lynn-margulis-your-cells-run-on-captured.context_blurb:
Inside nearly every cell of your body are hundreds of mitochondria, tiny power plants that burn food to make usable energy. In 1967 Lynn Margulis, a young American biologist, proposed that they began as free-living bacteria, swallowed by a larger cell some two billion years ago. Mocked at first, the idea is now in every biology textbook.

She liked to put it simply: long ago an amoeba ate a bacterium but could not digest it, and the bacterium lived on inside, making itself useful. Her paper, signed Lynn Sagan, appeared in 1967 only after about fifteen journals had rejected it, by her own recollection.

The clues are inside you. Mitochondria carry their own small loop of DNA, and you inherited it only from your mother, through the egg; sperm contribute essentially none. That DNA is one continuous closed circle, the way bacteria carry theirs, unlike the long straight chromosomes of the nucleus. And a cell cannot build a new mitochondrion from parts: each one comes from an existing mitochondrion pinching in two, just as a bacterium divides.

The evidence came before the theory. In 1963 Margit and Sylvan Nass photographed fine threads inside chick mitochondria with an electron microscope, and showed they were DNA when an enzyme that destroys DNA dissolved them away. Forty years before Margulis, the anatomist Ivan Wallin had claimed to grow mitochondria from rabbit liver as if they were bacteria, but biologists objected that a single stray germ in a dish could have produced his result. His idea was right; his evidence was not.

Such partnerships can form fast. In 1966 bacteria infected Kwang Jeon's laboratory amoebas; most died, but a few survived, still packed with bacteria. When Jeon later killed the bacteria with drugs, the amoebas sickened and died soon afterwards, because the lodgers had begun making a protein the host now needed.

Margulis met scorn. Harvard's Keith Porter asked her with a sneer whether she believed in acquired characteristics and in macromutation, two ideas a Darwinist of 1967 filed with the cranks: traits picked up during a lifetime being inherited, and evolution by sudden leaps. She said later that her ideas were not controversial; they were right.

The bacterial past has a cost at the pharmacy. Mitochondria still use small, bacterial-style ribosomes, so antibiotics such as linezolid and the aminoglycosides, which jam bacterial ribosomes, can also jam the ribosomes inside a patient's mitochondria, causing side effects such as deafness. The original bacterium probably carried around a thousand genes; human mitochondrial DNA now holds just 37, because most of the rest moved into the host cell's nucleus.

Margulis was not right about everything. Her 1967 paper also claimed that the whiplike tails called flagella came from captured spirochete bacteria, but no leftover genome was ever found, and biologists now trace flagella to copies of genes already present in the cell.

Open questions remain. Mitochondrial genes sit within one bacterial family, but on which branch? A 2011 study put them beside SAR11, the ocean's most abundant bacteria, and critics answered that the method had been fooled because both groups had drifted toward genomes heavy in the letters A and T, a resemblance that is not kinship. No one yet knows. The list of captured organelles is growing: in 2024 scientists found a third in a sea alga, the nitroplast, a former bacterium that pulls nitrogen straight out of the air for its host. And in 2020 Hiroyuki Imachi's team, after twelve years of patient culturing, finally grew an Asgard archaeon, a relative of the cell that swallowed the first mitochondrion. The cell sprouted long, branching arms, hinting at how a host might first have grabbed its guest.

lysenko-the-terminus-of-state-enforced-s.context_blurb:
Trofim Lysenko, a Soviet agronomist from a peasant family, rose in the 1930s to become the farm scientist Stalin trusted most, by promising bigger harvests without genetics, which he rejected as bourgeois. His rise shows what happens when a state decides what science must find: testing is thrown out, and dissenters pay with their lives.

His signature trick was chilling damp wheat seed close to freezing so that winter wheat could be sown in spring; he called it vernalization. Chilling seed was already known to European farmers. Lysenko's leap was the claim that seeds saved from a treated plant would grow into plants that inherited the new trait, so that nature could be re-educated.

He mocked his opponents, the Mendelian geneticists, as Weismannist-Morganists, and as fly-lovers, after the fruit flies their science was built on. He ran his trials without control groups and refused statistics altogether, dismissing them as bourgeois formalism; with no honest numbers, nothing could ever show him wrong.

When his methods failed, Lysenko blamed people. From 1936 he accused Nikolai Vavilov, the country's greatest geneticist who had assembled the world's first great collection of crop seeds, of sabotage, a charge that under Stalin could mean death. Vavilov was arrested in 1940, and in 1943 the man who had gathered seeds to end famine was slowly starved to death in prison. His staff in besieged Leningrad starved guarding the seed collection rather than eat it.

In August 1948, at a Moscow meeting presented as a scientific debate, Lysenko told the hall that the Party Central Committee had examined and approved his report, and the room rose in an ovation. Afterwards Mendelian genetics could not legally be taught in the USSR.

Nature did not obey. Under Stalin's 1948 plan to plant great forest belts, Lysenko had crews sow acorns in tight nests, claiming that plants of one species do not compete; the forest ecologist Vladimir Sukachev quietly recorded a survival rate of about 10 per cent. And in 1955 Khrushchev, needing maize that grew, bought seed from the Iowa farmer Roswell Garst: high-yield lines that were the direct product of Mendelian genetics, the very science Lysenko had outlawed.

mandates-consent-and-the-line-from-jacob.context_blurb:
When smallpox reached Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1902, the board of health required its adults to be vaccinated. One man's refusal produced a Supreme Court case still cited today, and twenty-two years later the same precedent was used to justify sterilising a young woman against her will. The line between them runs through the question of consent.

The board's order covered every inhabitant who had not been successfully vaccinated within the past five years, so even a man vaccinated as a boy had to go again. The penalty under Massachusetts law was mild: an adult who refused could be made to pay five dollars, and nothing in the law allowed anyone to be vaccinated by force.

The Lutheran pastor Henning Jacobson, born in Sweden, refused. His reason was personal: as a child, he said, a vaccination had left him gravely ill for a long time, and his son had reacted badly too. Convicted, he kept appealing until the Supreme Court heard him.

In 1905 Justice John Marshall Harlan upheld the order and answered Jacobson's claim seriously. Real liberty for all, he wrote, cannot exist under a principle that lets each person use himself as he likes, whatever harm others suffer. That is the strongest case for compulsion in American law. But Harlan also wrote in a limit that short summaries drop: a court could refuse to enforce the order for a man to whom vaccination would be cruel and inhuman.

Jacobson was about an adult and a five-dollar fine. School rules came to the Court in 1922, when Rosalyn Zucht was turned away from a San Antonio school, and the justices held that a school may bar an unvaccinated child even with no epidemic under way.

In 1927 Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. wrote for an 8-1 majority in Buck v. Bell, upholding Virginia's sterilisation of Carrie Buck, a young woman confined in a state colony. For his precedent he reached for Jacobson: the principle that let a state compel smallpox vaccination, he wrote, also covered sterilisation. The case was rigged. The historian Paul Lombardo found that her own lawyer, Irving Whitehead, had once sat on the colony's board; he called no witnesses for her.

Buck v. Bell has never been overruled. In 1942 the Court, with Justice William O. Douglas writing, threw out an Oklahoma law that sterilised a man convicted of larceny but exempted an embezzler who took the same money, without touching Buck at all.

By then the world was writing down the opposite principle. At Nuremberg, American judges tried Nazi doctors for their experiments on human beings, and in their verdict of August 1947 the three judges themselves wrote the ten-point Nuremberg Code. Its first rule is the only one they made absolute: a person's voluntary consent to being experimented on is required, with no exception. Whether a treatment works is a question for evidence; whether a person may be compelled to take it is a separate question.

mapping-the-mind-by-what-breaks.context_blurb:
One of the oldest ways to learn what a part of the brain does is to watch what stops working when that part is damaged. This lesion logic has mapped speech, memory and the brain's left and right sides, and it keeps overturning tidy stories, including some popular ones.

For twenty-one years a patient in a Paris hospital, Louis Victor Leborgne, understood what people said to him but could utter just one syllable, tan. When he died in 1861, the surgeon Paul Broca examined his brain and found a single small area of damage at the rear of the left frontal lobe. Speaking and understanding were separate jobs in separate places. One case is only an anecdote, so after a second patient, Broca collected twelve more autopsies over the next two years, and every lesion sat in the same place. In 1865 he concluded that we speak with the left hemisphere.

Wilder Penfield, a surgeon in Montreal in the mid-twentieth century, operated on epileptic patients who stayed awake, because brain tissue itself cannot feel pain; only the scalp needed numbing. Touching an electrode to the exposed cortex, he asked what they felt. A secretary heard music, and afterwards she tracked down the sheet music and played the tune on the piano. Such vivid replays were rare: by one count, only 40 people out of 520 he operated on ever relived a memory, though headlines called the brain a tape recorder. With Edwin Boldrey, Penfield mapped the body along a groove of the cortex, and the map came out lopsided, with huge lips, tongue, hands and fingers, because territory goes to the parts most richly wired for touch and fine control.

Lesions also kill a popular myth. The claim that we use only ten percent of our brains is refuted most directly by the fact that damage to almost any patch of brain costs a patient some ability. The brain burns up to a fifth of the body's energy, and evolution does not pay for idle tissue.

William Beecher Scoville, a surgeon, cut tissue from both sides of Henry Molaison's brain in 1953 to stop his seizures. They stopped, and his intelligence and conversation stayed intact, but the operation destroyed his power to lay down lasting memories of anything new. The psychologist Brenda Milner had him trace a star seen only in a mirror. Over three days his errors fell from about thirty to almost none, yet each time he insisted he had never tried the task before in his life. Memory is not one thing: the facts-and-events kind needed the hippocampi Scoville removed, while the skill kind ran through the cerebellum and the basal ganglia, which he never touched.

For severe epilepsy, surgeons sometimes cut the corpus callosum, the cable joining the brain's two halves. Afterwards the patients said they felt exactly the same as they always had. The strangeness appeared only in the laboratory. Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga flashed a picture to a patient's silent right hemisphere; he truthfully said he had seen nothing, yet his left hand reached into a hidden bag and pulled out exactly that object. When one patient's left hand picked a shovel to match a snow scene only his right hemisphere had seen, his speaking left hemisphere instantly invented a reason: a shovel was needed for mucking out the chicken shed. The popular split into left-brained logical people and right-brained creative people does not follow. Brain scans of ordinary people reading, doing sums or hearing music show both halves working the same task as one network.

mariottes-hole-in-your-sight.context_blurb:
There is a blind spot in each of your eyes. Where the bundle of nerve fibres leaves the eyeball, there are no light-sensitive cells at all, because the vertebrate eye is wired with its cables running in front of its sensors. The octopus eye, wired the other way, has no such gap.

In 1668 the French priest Mariotte, one of the first members of the French Academy of Sciences, described this patch, the blind spot, overturning the old belief that the entire retina responds to light. He mapped the blind patch with small circles of white paper. Test it yourself: close one eye, stare at a mark on a page, and slide the page until a dot nearby vanishes.

Yet you never see a hole. Your brain covers it by filling the gap with the pattern around it, running stripes across stripes and blue across blue; it does not invent new objects to put there.

matter-is-a-wave-de-broglies-guess-and-t.context_blurb:
In 1924 a young French physicist, Louis de Broglie, proposed that matter itself travels as a wave: if light can behave like particles, then particles such as electrons should behave like waves. Within a few years a lucky laboratory accident in America proved him right.

His examiners in Paris did not know what to make of his doctoral thesis, so his adviser Paul Langevin sent it to Albert Einstein. Einstein replied in December 1924 that the young Frenchman had raised one corner of the great veil, and that praise got the idea taken seriously. The Austrian physicist Erwin Schrödinger read the thesis in 1925, became convinced that particles really are waves, and built his wave equation on that idea, an equation chemists still rely on.

De Broglie's formula says a particle's wavelength is Planck's constant divided by its momentum. For a walking person that comes to about 10^-35 metres, far too small to matter, which is why people never diffract when they walk through a doorway. Electrons are light and slow enough for their waves to show.

The proof came by accident. Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer, studying electron scattering at Bell Labs in 1925, were aiming electrons at heated nickel in a vacuum tube when a flask of liquid air above the apparatus broke, cracked the equipment and let in air that coated the nickel with oxide. To clean it they baked the nickel for weeks, and the long heating fused its many tiny grains into a few large single crystals. When they restarted, the electrons bounced off in sharp peaks at angles fitting the rule William Henry and Lawrence Bragg had worked out in 1913 for X-rays scattering off crystal planes. The electrons were arriving as waves.

Davisson shared the 1937 Nobel Prize with George Paget Thomson, who made electrons ring out diffraction patterns through thin metal foil. George's father, J. J. Thomson, had earned his own Nobel in 1906 by using cathode rays to show that the electron is a corpuscle with a definite ratio of charge to mass. The father proved it a particle and the son proved it a wave, and both were right.

The short wavelength is now a tool. Green light's wavelength is about 550 nanometres, but an electron sped up to 100 kilovolts has a wavelength some hundred thousand times smaller, so an electron microscope can picture single atoms in a crystal lattice, which no light microscope can resolve.

maxwell-the-number-that-turned-out-to-be.context_blurb:
In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell, a Scottish physicist, worked out how fast a disturbance in electric and magnetic fields would travel, and the answer came out at the speed of light. Light, he concluded, is an electromagnetic wave. Richard Feynman later said that, judged ten millennia from now, this would be the greatest event of the nineteenth century, and that the American Civil War of the same decade would pale beside it.

Michael Faraday pictured magnetism as curved lines of force, made visible with iron filings, but he could not write equations for them. In essays of 1855 and 1856 the young Maxwell put numbers on the lines by imagining each one as a pipe carrying a fluid that cannot be compressed, so the mathematics of flowing liquids could be carried over to magnetism.

In 1861 Maxwell built a mechanical picture of space packed with spinning vortices and tiny rolling particles, like the small idler gears between big wheels, and then wrote, in the same paper, that he did not put it forward as the way nature actually works. Still, he turned its crank and a speed came out. The inputs to that calculation all came from Wilhelm Weber and Rudolf Kohlrausch, who in 1856 had measured the charge in a Leyden jar twice, once by the force it exerts and once by the current it makes; their experiment used no light at all. Maxwell's answer, 310,740 kilometres a second, landed inside the spread of the measured speeds of light. The three rival measurements of light disagreed with each other by more than any of them disagreed with his number, and he had worked out his equations before he knew how close they would come.

His key addition solved a puzzle in a charging capacitor: current flows in the wire, but no charge crosses the space between its plates, so the law linking magnetism to current gave two answers. Maxwell ruled that the electric field between the plates, as it changes, counts as a current too, and called it the displacement current. That one term is why light exists in the equations: a changing electric field makes a magnetic field, whose change makes an electric field, and the wave regenerates itself across empty space.

His 1864 paper did not contain the four neat equations of the textbooks. It held twenty equations to be solved together, in twenty unknown quantities. The self-taught Oliver Heaviside, partly deaf from scarlet fever and out of school at sixteen, cut them down to four in 1884 by throwing out the potentials, quantities from which fields are calculated, and keeping only the fields themselves.

In 1887 at Karlsruhe, Heinrich Hertz drove a spark across a gap between two copper wires, and metres away a plain loop of wire with a narrow slit, connected to nothing, showed a tiny spark jumping across its slit: the first electromagnetic waves made on purpose. When his students asked what use the waves might be, Hertz reportedly said they were of no use whatsoever.

You can test Maxwell's claim at home. Point a TV remote at a phone's selfie camera in a dark room and press a button: your eyes see nothing, but the screen shows a flash, because the camera picks up an infrared pulse, the same kind of wave as visible light but longer. Or remove a microwave oven's spinning plate and melt a flat bar of chocolate: the soft patches sit about six centimetres apart, which is half of one wavelength, so doubling that and multiplying by the oven's frequency gives the speed of light.

Maxwell believed his waves rippled through an invisible ether filling space. Edward Morley and Albert Michelson in 1887 floated a delicate instrument on mercury in Cleveland and turned it slowly to catch Earth's motion through that ether, and found no measurable drift whichever way the instrument faced. The equations survived; the ether did not.

maxwells-demon-and-the-price-of-one-bit.context_blurb:
In an 1867 letter, James Clerk Maxwell pictured a little gatekeeper minding a trapdoor in a wall that divides a box of gas. It lets fast molecules through one way and slow ones the other, so one side grows hot and the other cold with no work done. Lord Kelvin later nicknamed the creature a demon.

Such sorting seems to break thermodynamics' second law, which says heat does not flow from cold to hot by itself. But Maxwell was not trying to overthrow the law. He was showing that it holds only statistically, for vast numbers of molecules in bulk, and does not forbid any single molecule from moving the wrong way.

In 1929 Leo Szilard shrank the puzzle to a cylinder holding a single molecule and showed that the demon could not work for nothing: the step of learning which side the molecule sat on must cost entropy. Information has a physical price. In 1961 the IBM physicist Rolf Landauer showed that wiping one bit of memory has an unavoidable minimum heat cost. In 2012 Antoine Bérut and colleagues in France and Germany measured that floor, using a single 2-micrometre silica bead trapped between two wells of laser light, the bead's position standing for the bit. Today's computer chips are nowhere near the limit: they release orders of magnitude more heat per bit than it demands.

mayer-and-the-bright-red-blood-of-the-tr.context_blurb:
In 1840 Julius Robert Mayer, a young German ship's doctor, sailed to Java and noticed something in a bucket of blood that led him to one of the great ideas of physics: heat, work and the energy in food are one quantity in different forms, and the total is conserved. Being right cost him dearly.

Bleeding sick sailors in the tropics, he found their venous blood, which has already passed through the body's tissues, nearly as bright red as arterial blood. He reasoned that in the heat their bodies were burning less food to make their own warmth, so less oxygen had been taken out of the blood. Warmth from outside could stand in for warmth burned within.

In 1841 he sent his first physics paper to the editor of the top German physics journal, Johann Christian Poggendorff, who never answered and never published it; it turned up in Poggendorff's papers 36 years later. Mayer's figure for how much work a unit of heat is worth did not come from an apparatus of his own: he calculated it from heat measurements other scientists had already published for gases, which made him easy for experimenters to dismiss.

In 1848 two of his children died, and Joule's supporters in England denied that Mayer had been first. In 1850 he threw himself from an upstairs window. He survived, but spent the following years in a series of asylum confinements. Rescue came in 1862, when the Irish physicist John Tyndall, lecturing at London's Royal Institution, credited the idea of energy to a man his audience had scarcely heard of: a German doctor named Mayer. The Royal Society awarded Mayer its Copley Medal in 1871.

mcclintocks-jumping-genes.context_blurb:
Barbara McClintock, an American geneticist, read surprises off corn cobs: kernels speckled and streaked with colour where none should be. In 1950 she published her explanation, that pieces of chromosome can move, and it took biology decades to catch up.

For fifty years geneticists had pictured genes as beads on a string, fixed in a fixed order. McClintock's shock was that some of the beads could get up and travel along the string. She traced the speckling to two pieces that work as a team, which she named Dissociation and Activator: one lands inside a colour gene and switches it off, and the other can pop it back out, so every cell descended from that moment makes colour again.

At the 1951 Cold Spring Harbor Symposium her talk met puzzlement rather than argument; she was not shunned so much as not followed. Nor was she a forgotten outcast: in 1945 she became the first woman president of the Genetics Society of America. Colleagues resisted her claim, not her standing.

Proof came from bacteria. In 1968 researchers found small mobile pieces of DNA, insertion sequences, jumping around the chromosomes of Escherichia coli. Through the 1970s such transposons turned up in species after species, and in 1983 McClintock alone received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Once transposons were accepted, scientists totted up the human genome and found that about half of it is built from transposons and their broken leftovers.

What are they for? In 1980 two papers in Nature, by Leslie Orgel and Francis Crick and by Ford Doolittle and Carmen Sapienza, argued that transposons are mostly selfish freeloaders, copying themselves at the cell's expense, the opposite of McClintock's view of them as controllers. The honest answer is that both happen.

mechains-error-and-the-metre-cut-from-th.context_blurb:
In 1791 the French Academy of Sciences defined a new unit of length, the metre, as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator along the meridian through Paris. The unit was to be cut from the planet itself, and two astronomers spent seven years measuring it.

The commission first rejected a rival standard, a pendulum measured so that each swing takes one second: since gravity varies from place to place, the same pendulum's length would differ between towns. Then, from 1792 to 1798, Pierre Méchain and Jean-Baptiste Delambre surveyed the meridian between Dunkirk and Barcelona.

France was in the midst of revolution. The two men hauled brass instruments up church towers and hilltops, and suspicious villagers repeatedly had them arrested as spies for the royalists. Their key instrument was Borda's repeating circle, built in 1784, which measured the same angle again and again around a graduated ring so that random errors shrank.

At Barcelona, Méchain measured the latitude from two stations, a fortress and an inn. The readings differed by some three seconds of arc, equal to about a hundred metres of ground. Unable to account for it, he concealed the second set and altered his notebooks to shrink the gap. The secret tormented him for the rest of his life.

Modern analysis largely clears him. Nearby mountains pull a plumb line sideways, so "straight down" does not point at the Earth's centre, an effect called deflection of the vertical, and it accounts for most of the metre's shortfall. The metre is slightly short of its definition, but the world kept it, because a standard's job is to be shared.

meitners-christmas-walk-fission-worked-o.context_blurb:
In the last days of 1938, on a snowy walk in Sweden, a refugee explained one of the strangest results chemistry had ever produced. Lise Meitner, an Austrian-born Jewish physicist who had fled Nazi Germany that summer, showed that a uranium atom can split in two and release enormous energy. The honours went elsewhere.

Meitner had worked in Berlin for thirty years, much of it beside the chemist Otto Hahn. When the regime barred her from leaving, she slipped out by train in July 1938 with two small suitcases, and Dirk Coster, a physicist from the Netherlands, saw her over the border. Hahn handed her a diamond ring that had been his mother's, to sell if money ran out.

The puzzle went back to 1934, when Enrico Fermi announced that neutrons fired into uranium had made new elements heavier than uranium. Ida Noddack, a German chemist, suggested the nucleus had burst into big pieces instead, but with no mechanism and no energy sums, nobody listened. Hahn, Meitner and Fritz Strassmann themselves wrote seven papers between 1935 and 1938 chasing Fermi's heavy new elements, which did not exist.

Then, in December 1938, a product Hahn and Strassmann had taken for radium refused to behave like radium. It behaved like barium, an element little more than half uranium's weight. Hahn wrote that he could not explain it. Meitner answered with doubt and an open door: so complete a breakup seemed very hard to accept, but nuclear physics had brought so many surprises that she would not call it impossible. Their paper of 22 December gave the chemistry in full, then stopped. As nuclear chemists close to physics, they wrote, they could not yet bring themselves to take a step that broke with all earlier experience.

At Kungälv that Christmas, Meitner and her nephew, the physicist Otto Frisch, argued over Hahn's news in the snow, Frisch on skis and Meitner walking. When the argument needed numbers, the two sat down on a fallen tree trunk and worked the sums on scraps of paper.

Niels Bohr had imagined a heavy nucleus as a liquid drop, held round by something like surface tension. A captured neutron might set the drop quivering until it stretched into a dumbbell. Uranium's nucleus is crammed with protons that all push on one another, so once the drop stretched far enough, their electric repulsion would beat the surface tension and pinch it in two. Meitner worked out that the two fragments together weighed less than the uranium by about a fifth of a proton's mass. Frisch ran that missing mass through Einstein's E=mc², and it came to about 200 million electron-volts per splitting atom, roughly a hundred million times what burning releases from each atom.

In Copenhagen early in 1939, Frisch needed a name. He asked a colleague what biologists call it when a living cell divides in two, heard "binary fission", and borrowed the word. A fragment carrying that energy should give a pulse far bigger than anything else uranium makes, but uranium also sprays out alpha particles constantly. So on 13 January he turned up his counter's trigger level until no alpha particle was strong enough to set it off. The giant pulses appeared exactly as predicted.

When the British team bound for Los Alamos invited Meitner to join, she still had no laboratory, money or secure post. She refused flatly, saying she would have nothing to do with a bomb.

The Royal Swedish Academy held back the 1944 chemistry prize until November 1945, and then a slim majority gave it to Hahn alone, for discovering how heavy nuclei split. Fifty years later the historians Ruth Lewin Sime, Elisabeth Crawford and Mark Walker published what that file held: no reasoned judgement against Meitner, only evaluators lost on a discovery that crossed two sciences, committees weak in theory, and wartime isolation. The ugliest cause lay in the record itself: Nazi rules had kept her name off the German papers she had helped produce, so the evidence the committee read was already bent against her. The failure was the committees', not Hahn's.

Element 109, first made one atom at a time at Darmstadt in 1982, was named meitnerium in 1997. Curium honours Marie and Pierre Curie together, so meitnerium is the only element named for a real woman alone. Meitner lies in the churchyard at Bramley in Hampshire, and Frisch chose the words cut into her stone: Lise Meitner, a physicist who never lost her humanity.

mendel-and-the-28-000-pea-plants.context_blurb:
Gregor Mendel was an Augustinian friar of the Abbey of St Thomas in Brno, Moravia, and a part-time science teacher. From 1856 to 1863 he crossed and counted roughly 28,000 pea plants in the abbey's vegetable garden. Out of those counts came the laws of heredity, though almost nobody noticed for thirty-four years.

His first subjects were mice, grey and white ones bred in his room to watch coat colour pass down, until, as the story goes, his bishop objected that a monk had no business breeding animals that mate. The tale comes from later tellings, not Mendel's papers, but it sent him to plants. His career was stuck too. For thirteen years he taught at the Brünn technical school only as a substitute, because he failed the teaching-certificate exam twice, the second time after studying physics in Vienna under Christian Doppler.

Before making a single cross, he spent two seasons growing 34 pea varieties, letting each fertilise itself to see whether it gave back the same form year after year. Only the 22 that bred true went forward, because only a reliable parent makes a hybrid's behaviour readable. Peas fertilise themselves inside the closed flower, so every cross meant surgery. Mendel opened each bud with tweezers and cut out its anthers, the pollen-bearing parts, before they could shed, then dusted on pollen from his chosen father and bagged the flower against insects.

Naturalists expected a cross between true round-seeded and true wrinkled-seeded peas to give something in between. Mendel's hybrids held round seeds only, with no wrinkle anywhere. He let those hybrids fertilise themselves and counted their offspring seed by seed: 5,474 round and 1,850 wrinkled, close to three to one. His other traits came out near three to one as well, never exactly.

That return killed blending, the doctrine everyone took for granted, which held that parents' traits mix in their young like paints and can never be separated again. Under blending, the wrinkled form should have been diluted for good. Instead it hid for a generation and came back whole, so heredity must travel in separate units.

Next he crossed peas that differed in two traits, shape and colour. The four combinations came out near 9:3:3:1, which is simply two three-to-one splits multiplied together: shape and colour were being handed out independently, neither paying any attention to the other. In his 1866 paper Mendel called the inherited units "differing cell elements". The word "gene" came only in 1909, long after his death, but "dominant" and "recessive" are his.

He mailed it to the celebrated botanist Carl Naegeli. Naegeli scrawled that it was merely empirical, not rational, never discussed the counts, and urged Mendel to repeat everything in hawkweed, the plant Naegeli himself specialised in. From 1869 Mendel did, dissecting florets so tiny that the work nearly ruined his eyes. No clean ratios came, and Mendel faulted his own clumsy fingers. The plant was the real problem: many hawkweed seeds form without any fertilisation, as copies of the mother, so their traits never get reshuffled.

Mendel died in 1884. In 1900 Carl Correns, Hugo de Vries and Erich von Tschermak each found the same ratios on his own, in four-o'clocks, evening primroses and peas, and each then discovered the forgotten Brno paper.

In 1936 the statistician R. A. Fisher ran chi-square tests on Mendel's tables and found them too good: fits so close to theory had odds near one in twenty thousand. Rather than accuse Mendel, Fisher suggested that some assistant who knew too well what was expected had fooled him. The laws survived the audit. Modern repeats of the crosses give Mendel's patterns, and a 2020 recheck found his fit within what honest experiment can produce.

The wrinkle itself was explained in 1990. A stretch of jumping DNA had broken a gene whose enzyme packs sugar away as starch. Left with nearly twice the sugar, the growing seed soaks up extra water and swells, and as it dries the swollen seed caves in and wrinkles.

mendeleev-leaves-holes-in-the-table.context_blurb:
Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian chemist in St Petersburg, published his periodic table in 1869. Others had sorted the elements by weight; his daring was to leave empty squares and describe, in advance, the elements that would fill them. Those predictions were then tested against real metals, and in time so were his mistakes.

He was not the first to seek order. In 1862 the French geologist Alexandre-Émile Béguyer de Chancourtois wound the elements by weight around a cylinder in a spiral, so that chemical cousins lined up one above another. The journal printed his paper without the drawing, nobody could follow it, and the idea sank. None of the early schemes dared to predict a missing element.

The tale that the table came to Mendeleev in a dream does not fit his own drafts, which show long sessions of sorting cards, one per element, the way a player lays out a game of patience. Each empty square got a placeholder name by one rule: the element sitting directly above it, plus a Sanskrit counting word. Eka-aluminium meant "one place below aluminium".

For that square Mendeleev wrote out a specification in 1871: atomic weight near 68, density 5.9, a low melting point. Four years later Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, hunting with a spectroscope, caught two violet lines in zinc ore from the Pyrenees and announced gallium. His laboratory sat upstairs in the family house in Cognac, paid for by the family business of distilling brandy. The melting point was right: gallium melts at about 30 degrees Celsius, so a lump held in a warm hand slumps into a silvery puddle. The density was not, at first. Boisbaudran measured 4.7, and Mendeleev, who had never seen the metal, published a note from St Petersburg saying the sample must still be impure and the true density was 5.9. Boisbaudran was furious, but he purified his speck again and got 5.9.

Scandium followed in 1879, when Lars Fredrik Nilson at Uppsala isolated its oxide without realising that Mendeleev had foretold it as eka-boron. Per Teodor Cleve, who worked in the same building, recognised the match and wrote to Mendeleev. The predicted density was off by about 0.3 percent.

In 1886 Clemens Winkler of the Freiberg Mining Academy analysed a silver mineral, argyrodite. His silver, sulfur and traces added up to only about 93 percent of the sample, a little over nine-tenths. Rather than blame sloppy work, he trusted his balance and hunted down the missing few percent: a new element. He wanted to call it neptunium, because the planet Neptune had been calculated from the tugs on Uranus's orbit before astronomers ever saw it, just as this element had been foretold before anyone dug it out. The name was taken, so he chose germanium, for his homeland. Even then nobody knew its square. Winkler put it between antimony and bismuth, and Mendeleev placed it under cadmium. The square under silicon was named by Lothar Meyer, author of a rival periodic table. There the metal matched the fifteen-year-old prediction almost perfectly.

Mendeleev trusted ghosts too. A green line seen in the Sun's corona during the 1869 eclipse matched nothing on Earth, and astronomers credited it to a new element, coronium. That was a fair guess, since helium had been found in the Sun first. Walter Grotrian and Bengt Edlén solved it in the 1930s: the line came from iron with 13 of its 26 electrons stripped away by the corona's heat of millions of degrees.

His confidence also led him astray. In a 1902 book on the ether, the invisible medium physicists thought carried light, he set two elements lighter than hydrogen ahead of it in his table, newtonium and coronium, to be the ether's stuff. Nothing can be that light; a single proton outweighs either.

Tellurium was his most stubborn bet. Its chemistry placed it before iodine, but it weighed more, so Mendeleev declared the weighing wrong, as he had rightly done for other elements. His own assistant spent years trying to drive the number down. The new weighings stood: tellurium, at 127.6, outweighs iodine at 126.9. His order was right and his reason wrong, because weight was never the table's true rule.

mercurys-stubborn-43-arcseconds-and-the-.context_blurb:
Mercury travels a stretched ellipse whose closest point to the Sun creeps slowly forward. In the nineteenth century astronomers found it creeping slightly too fast for Newton's gravity. The hunt for the cause ran from a phantom planet to Albert Einstein.

The phantom's champion was Urbain Le Verrier. In 1846 Uranus was straying from its predicted path, so Le Verrier calculated where an unseen outer planet must be pulling from. Johann Galle in Berlin aimed there and found Neptune that very night, within a degree of the spot.

In 1859 Le Verrier turned to Mercury. Its extra creep was far too small to watch directly, so he built it up from timings of Mercury's transits across the Sun's disc, fourteen of them reaching back to 1697. Each transit can be timed to the second, and a century and a half of them exposed about 38 arcseconds per century that nothing explained; Simon Newcomb later refined the leftover to 43.

Le Verrier reached for his proven trick and proposed a small planet inside Mercury's orbit, soon named Vulcan. A country doctor at Orgères, Edmond Lescarbault, had seen a black dot cross the Sun from his rooftop observatory. Lacking proper instruments, he timed it with the pendulum he used to count his patients' pulses and an old clock. Le Verrier took the train out, grilled him, and declared the planet confirmed, and Emperor Napoleon III made the doctor a Chevalier of the Légion d'honneur.

Le Verrier then named the dates when Vulcan would next cross the Sun. Observers watched, and on none of those dates did anything cross. A claim that names dates can be killed by the sky, which is what makes it science. By the mid-1870s every transit and every daytime sighting had failed, yet Le Verrier would not let go. He shattered his one planet into a cloud of little bodies, each too small to be seen. That move is worth spotting: a failed testable claim reshaped into one that is harder to test. He died in 1877 still convinced.

Sightings kept coming. During the total eclipse of July 1878, James Craig Watson in Wyoming and Lewis Swift near Denver both reported a reddish object near the Sun, but their positions disagreed, and both turned out to be ordinary stars in the constellation Cancer. Watson then had a slanting shaft dug into a Wisconsin hillside, with a telescope below and a mirror above, trusting the ancient folk belief that stars can be seen by day from the bottom of a well. The belief is false, since scattered skylight fills a shaft too, and Watson died with the shaft unfinished.

The answer was a new law, not a new planet. In June 1913 Einstein and his friend Michele Besso ran Mercury through a draft of Einstein's gravity theory. Once an early blunder was fixed, the draft delivered only about 18 of the 43 arcseconds, so Mercury had shown it was wrong. In November 1915 his finished general relativity produced the full 43. Einstein told Paul Ehrenfest the result had given him palpitations of the heart, and that he was beside himself with joy for days.

Every rival explanation had a dial: choose the mass of a hidden planet or the flattening of the Sun, and you could make it give 43. Einstein's term depended only on the Sun's mass and the size and shape of Mercury's orbit, with no adjustable quantity to fit, so his number was fixed before anyone compared it.

The 43 hides inside a far bigger number. Measured against the equinox, Mercury's closest point advances about 5,600 arcseconds a century, but some 5,025 of those are not Mercury moving at all: the equinox itself slides as Earth's own axis wheels slowly round, dragging the reference point along. Subtract that, then about 532 for the pull of the other planets, and 43 remains.

The last rival was a Sun bulging at its equator, which would turn Mercury's orbit by itself. The bulge was too slight to measure until 2017, when Park and colleagues used radio ranging to the MESSENGER spacecraft circling Mercury and found it far too small to matter.

So the rule that found Neptune failed at Mercury for a deep reason: Newton's gravity, the very law used to subtract the known pulls, was itself incomplete. An anomaly can mean a missing object or a broken law, and only a test can say which.

meselson-and-stahl-the-most-beautiful-ex.context_blurb:
By the mid-1950s biologists knew DNA was a double helix but not how it copies itself. One idea, the conservative model, kept the parent molecule whole and built a fresh one beside it. Others had the two strands part, or old and new pieces chopped and shuffled together. Argument could not choose between them, so an experiment had to.

Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl, working at Caltech in 1958, built one that the biologist John Cairns called the most beautiful experiment in biology. Their trick was weight. They grew E. coli for about fourteen generations on food whose only nitrogen was nitrogen-15, a stable form one neutron heavier than ordinary nitrogen-14, until every nitrogen atom in the bacteria's DNA was the heavy kind. Nitrogen-15 is not radioactive, unlike the tags Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase had used in 1952, so nothing glowed; the centrifuge had to sort the DNA purely by its density.

To do it they spun the DNA for twenty hours in a solution of caesium chloride, a salt so heavy that the spinning packs it densest at the bottom of the tube. Each DNA molecule settles where the salt matches its own density and hangs there as a band.

Then they moved the heavy bacteria onto ordinary nitrogen and let them divide exactly once. The photograph showed a single band, precisely halfway between heavy and light, and no heavy band anywhere. That one picture killed the conservative model, which needs the original all-heavy double helix to come through copying intact. The other two ideas still fitted, and later generations would decide between them.

metchnikoffs-thorn-and-the-standing-army.context_blurb:
Élie Metchnikoff, a Russian zoologist, spent 1882 in Messina, Sicily, studying starfish larvae so transparent that he could watch everything inside them. He noticed cells drifting through their bodies and wondered whether they were guards that hunted down intruders. His test launched the study of the immune system's cells.

A larva has no blood vessels and no nerves, so if cells gathered at a wound, nothing but the cells themselves could have brought them there. Metchnikoff fetched thorns from a garden and pushed one under a larva's skin, as a man might run a splinter into his finger. Too excited to sleep, he looked at dawn: the wandering cells had heaped onto the thorn in clumps big enough to see without a microscope. He wrote that the zoologist became a pathologist that night.

Passing through Vienna, he asked Carl Claus, a zoologist who knew ancient Greek, to coin a name meaning devouring cells. The answer was phagocyte, from the words for "to eat" and "cell", and it has stuck.

Doctors then saw the redness, heat and swelling of an inflamed wound as the illness to be fought. In 1883 Metchnikoff argued the reverse: inflammation is what it looks like when the body's mobile cells are fighting microbes, a battle rather than the damage. He pictured the phagocytes as an army hurling itself on the enemy. That defied the textbooks, which taught that white cells, far from killing germs, ferried them about the body and gave them a good place to multiply. When the great pathologist Rudolf Virchow passed through Messina, he found the slides convincing but warned Metchnikoff to be careful.

The water flea Daphnia gave him a clear window on a whole infection. A fungus with needle-shaped spores pierces its gut, and the flea survives only if its wandering cells eat and digest the spores before they germinate; if the spores sprout first, the fungus spreads and the flea dies. Daphnia live in most ponds; a cheap microscope shows the fight.

In 1892, by then at Pasteur's institute, he wanted to prove the cholera germ alone could cause the disease, and no laboratory animal could catch it. So he drank down an entire flask of live cholera culture, and stayed well. A volunteer who swallowed an older culture fell gravely ill, and after a later volunteer died of an unexplained cause, Metchnikoff swore off human experiments.

The rival humoral school said immunity lived in the blood's fluid, and it had real evidence. In Munich in the late 1880s, Hans Buchner showed that cell-free serum killed anthrax germs; warming it a little past 56 °C wiped out that power, and adding fresh serum brought it straight back. The fragile killer, later called complement, is a team of proteins that unfold when heated. The school's heroes were Emil von Behring, with his diphtheria antitoxin, and its chief theorist, Paul Ehrlich. In 1908 the Nobel committee refused to pick a winner and split the prize between Metchnikoff and Ehrlich. Both sides were half right, and immunology still divides into fast inborn defences and slower ones that remember.

Ralph Steinman and Zanvil Cohn, in 1973, found a rare branching cell in mouse spleens, the dendritic cell. It barely ate anything, but it was 100 to 300 times better than ordinary spleen cells at rousing T cells that had never met their target. It links the two armies.

In 1989 Charles Janeway named immunology's "dirty little secret": a clean protein injected alone raises almost no antibodies, but mixed with crushed microbes it raises plenty. He argued the body must carry receptors tuned to molecular patterns that whole families of germs share and our own cells never make. Flies led to them. Jules Hoffmann's Strasbourg team showed in 1996 that flies with a broken Toll gene died of a mould, yet since 1985 Toll had been known only as a body-plan gene, the one that settles which side of a fly embryo becomes the underside. In 1998 Bruce Beutler found why one mouse strain ignored bacterial endotoxin: a single swapped letter in Tlr4, a relative of Toll that senses the toxin.

In 2011 the Nobel Assembly honoured Beutler, Hoffmann and Steinman. Steinman had fought pancreatic cancer with therapies built on his own discovery, and he died three days before the announcement. The rules bar prizes to the dead, but nobody had known, so the Nobel Foundation let the award stand, and his family collected it in Stockholm that December.

miasma-the-honest-wrong-consensus.context_blurb:
For some two thousand years doctors blamed epidemics on miasma: bad air rising from marshes, sewers, graveyards and rotting rubbish. It was a sensible theory held by serious people, and it was wrong. Yet the cleaning it demanded often saved lives anyway, because filth and germs really do travel together.

The theory survives inside a word. Malaria comes from old Italian for "bad air", because the fever clustered around marshes. The marshes were the right place to look and the wrong thing to blame: in 1897 the army doctor Ronald Ross showed in India that the disease passes by a mosquito's bite, and mosquitoes breed in still water.

In Britain the bad-air theory drove a great clean-up. Edwin Chadwick sent investigators out to count, and his 1842 report found that people in rural Rutland lived on average to 45, but in the new factory towns only to 26. In 1846 he told a Commons committee that every smell, if strong enough, simply is disease. His cause was wrong, yet nearly every remedy he demanded was right. Parliament's Public Health Act, passed in 1848, set up local boards of health with the power to build sewers and pipe in clean water.

In July 1855 the physicist Michael Faraday went out in a boat on the Thames and dropped scraps of white paper over the side, counting how fast they vanished in the murk. They disappeared almost at once. His letter to The Times calling the river a sewer was ignored. Anyone can repeat the test with paper, a bridge and a count.

Then came the hot June of 1858, the Great Stink, when the river beside Parliament was little more than a sewer. Members who feared bad air hung the river-facing windows with curtains soaked in chloride of lime, a disinfectant. The smell moved Parliament in weeks where argument had failed for years, and by August it had voted the money for Joseph Bazalgette's intercepting sewers. They were built to carry away the stench, and they carried away the cholera too. In London's last great cholera outbreak, in 1866, some 93 percent of the victims came from East End districts still waiting to be joined to the new sewers. Those districts differed in other ways too, and untangling which difference did the killing took decades.

Florence Nightingale, who ran the army hospital at Scutari in the Crimean War, was a committed miasmatist. She did not believe illness passed from person to person, and she blamed scarlet fever, measles and smallpox alike on foul air rising from a house's own drains. Her remedy of fresh air, light, warmth and cleanliness is still good nursing, and it worked for reasons she rejected. A treatment that works does not prove the theory behind it.

The statistician William Farr found that cholera deaths fell steadily the higher a London district stood above the Thames, as if bad air pooled low. The gradient was real, but altitude was a stand-in for water: low districts drew their supply from the foulest stretch of river, so elevation was really tracking which company's pipes fed each patch of ground. A hidden third factor like that is called a confounder, and it is why a strong correlation never proves a cause by itself.

The bad-air camp had real scientists in it. In Munich, Max von Pettenkofer, the first man anywhere to hold a chair of hygiene, devised a way of measuring the carbon dioxide in indoor air that stayed the standard test until 1958, the ancestor of the cheap CO2 meter you can carry into a stuffy classroom. He granted that Koch's germ existed but insisted it could never start an outbreak alone: the soil had to ripen it first, fermenting it as the ground water sank.

In October 1892, at seventy-four, he drank a broth of live cholera germs sent from Koch's own lab, with witnesses watching. First he swallowed sodium bicarbonate to neutralise his stomach acid, which would otherwise have killed the germs, so he was giving them their best chance. He had colic and diarrhoea but not cholera, declared germ theory beaten, and blamed the outcome on his missing soil condition. A theory with a spare part that can absorb any result has stopped predicting anything. Researchers today think a small dose, plus a partial immunity left by an earlier, milder infection, probably spared him. He was brave and sincere, he tested his claim on his own body, and he was still wrong.

michelson-morley-the-most-famous-nothing.context_blurb:
In 1887, in a basement in Cleveland, Ohio, Albert Michelson and Edward Morley ran the most sensitive optical experiment of its day, hunting an invisible substance that physicists were sure filled space. They found almost nothing, and that careful nothing helped clear the way for Einstein's relativity.

Every wave anyone knew of travelled through something: sound through air, ripples through water. So nineteenth-century physicists, Maxwell and Kelvin among them, took it for granted that light waves needed a medium too, an unseen one spread through all space and standing perfectly still. They called it the luminiferous ether.

Earth circles the Sun at about 30 kilometres a second, so it should feel a steady ether wind. Michelson's interferometer was built to catch it. It split a beam of light in two, sent the halves down arms at right angles, and brought them back together, where they formed a pattern of bright and dark stripes called fringes. If the wind slowed one half more than the other, turning the instrument would make those stripes shift.

His first try, at Potsdam near Berlin in 1881, came out unclear, and Hendrik Lorentz and Alfred Potier soon found a slip in it: Michelson had expected a fringe shift twice as large as the theory really predicted. Corrected, his instrument was barely sensitive enough. So in 1887 he and the chemist Edward Morley rebuilt it at Cleveland. Mirrors folded each beam to and fro across a stone only a few feet wide, stretching every arm to about 11 metres of light path, some ten times longer than before.

Turning the apparatus without a tremor was the hard part. They set it on a massive slab of sandstone and floated the slab on a pool of liquid mercury, dense enough to bear the stone and slick enough to let it turn smoothly by hand.

The ether theory called for a shift of roughly 0.4 of a fringe. The fringes moved less than 0.02 of a fringe: well under a twentieth of a fringe, and only a twentieth of what the ether demanded. Michelson himself saw it as a failure, and for years he suspected some botch in his own apparatus.

Physicists did not drop the ether at once. George FitzGerald in 1889, and Lorentz on his own in 1892, proposed that anything moving through it shrinks along its line of travel by exactly enough to hide the wind. That contraction was precise and testable, and it survives inside relativity.

In 1905 Albert Einstein cut the knot. Rather than explain why the ether hid, he discarded it and took the constant speed of light as a starting assumption, and the contraction then followed as a consequence. Einstein later gave mixed accounts of how much the 1887 result had influenced him.

The result is often called a null, as if nothing had been learned. That reading is wrong: a null result is a measured upper limit with an error bar, and a limit that tight rules out whole families of theories at once.

A positive signal can be an artefact too. In the 1920s Dayton Miller turned a similar instrument thousands of times on Mount Wilson and reported a small, steady ether drift. He was careful and honest, but his apparatus was not shielded from heat, and modern reanalysis traced his drift to temperature differences across the instrument.

milankovics-thirty-years-of-arithmetic.context_blurb:
Ice ages come and go on a schedule set by Earth's orbit. The man who did the sums was Milutin Milanković, a Serbian engineer and astronomer who spent decades calculating by hand how much sunlight reached each part of Earth across hundreds of thousands of years. He worked through two world wars, and proof came only after his death.

In June 1914 he married and took his bride to Dalj, his birthplace, then inside Austria-Hungary. Within weeks the war began, and because he was a reserve officer of the Serbian army, the Austrian police arrested him as an enemy. In his cell that first night he opened his little suitcase of papers and notes on the cosmic problem, found clean paper, and by his own memoir wrote until long after midnight.

After a spell in an internment camp, his old Vienna professor got him sent on Christmas Eve to Budapest, where he was confined to the city and reported to the police weekly. Szily, director of the Academy of Sciences library, heard of the prisoner, found him a desk among the Academy's books and let him work undisturbed.

There he repeated one calculation endlessly, with pen and paper and no machine. Each finished line gave one number: the sunlight reaching one latitude of Earth in one season of the distant past, a quantity called insolation. One set of tables took a hundred days. A laptop now does the whole job in a fraction of a second.

He was building on an older idea. In 1864 the Scot James Croll had put the ice ages down to Earth's orbit in a leading journal, although his day job in Glasgow was janitor at Anderson's University, sweeping and locking up; he taught himself physics from the library he looked after. Croll stressed long, cold winters. Milanković took up a different idea, first floated by Joseph John Murphy in 1869: an ice sheet grows when summers are too cool to melt away the previous winter's snow, because snow that survives one weak summer reflects sunlight and keeps the next summer cool too. So the number that mattered was summer sunlight at 65 degrees north, and putting a figure on it made the hunch testable.

His finished 626-page Canon of Insolation went to a Belgrade printer on 2 April 1941. Four days later German bombers destroyed the printing house, but almost all the printed sheets survived in its warehouse, and the book came out that same year. In May two German officers, geology students in uniform, called at his home bringing the good wishes of the Freiburg geologist Wolfgang Soergel. Milanković handed them the only full printed copy of the Canon to carry to Soergel, so that the work would survive whatever happened.

He died in 1958, a year after a geologist reportedly called his theory rubbish. In 1976 Nicholas Shackleton, John Imbrie and J. D. Hays tested it against the mud collecting on the deep-ocean floor, whose layers record the climate of the last 450,000 years. The beats were there, at about 23,000, 42,000 and 100,000 years, matching his orbital cycles.

One puzzle remains. The 100,000-year beat belongs to the weakest of the three wobbles, the stretching of Earth's orbit, which changes total sunlight by barely 0.2 watts per square metre, yet the ice of the past million years has kept its time. Earlier than roughly a million years back, the cores show, glaciations followed a quicker rhythm of about 41,000 years, the beat of Earth's axis tipping back and forth between about 22 and 24.5 degrees. Why the rhythm switched, and why the feeblest push moves the most ice, nobody yet knows.

millers-flask-and-the-honest-gap.context_blurb:
How did life begin? Nobody yet knows. In 1952 Stanley Miller, a Chicago graduate student of just twenty-two, turned the question into an experiment. He showed that ordinary chemistry can make some of life's building blocks, and his own results show honestly how far that still is from a living cell.

The idea had old roots. Writing to the botanist Joseph Hooker in 1871, Charles Darwin imagined life starting in some warm little pond, rich in ammonia, salts, light, heat and electricity. Darwin never published the guess; it survives because Hooker kept the letter. The Russian biochemist Alexander Oparin in 1924, and J. B. S. Haldane, a British biologist, in 1929, each proposed alone that simple gases in an oxygen-free early ocean could build richer and richer molecules until life appeared. Their shared picture of an early sea slowly thickening with organic matter earned a homely name: the primordial soup.

Miller's supervisor was Harold Urey, a Nobel-winning chemist who held that early Earth's air lacked free oxygen. Miller sealed hydrogen, methane, ammonia and steam into a glass loop with boiling water and ran electric sparks through it for a week, standing in for lightning over a young sea. The water turned a murky pink-brown, and analysis found amino acids, the building blocks of protein. Urey refused to put his name on the paper so that Miller would get the credit, but the work is still called the Miller-Urey experiment.

Miller could name the chemistry. The sparks broke his gases into two small, very reactive molecules, hydrogen cyanide and formaldehyde, and these joined with ammonia to make amino acids, by a route the chemist Adolph Strecker had found in 1850.

The honest accounting is less sunny. Only about two percent of the methane's carbon became amino acids, and most of the rest ended as a stubborn brown tar coating the glass. No sugars or nucleotides appeared. Geologists who read ancient rocks now think the early air was largely nitrogen and carbon dioxide, not methane and ammonia, and reruns with that mix give far fewer amino acids. The chemistry was real; the recipe may not have matched the young planet.

One more gap is still open. Every rerun, whether in warm ponds, deep-sea vents or on mineral surfaces, makes amino acids half left-handed and half right-handed, like mirror-image gloves. Living proteins use only the left-handed forms, and how life came to choose one hand is a puzzle no one has yet solved.

millers-thymus-and-glicks-chickens.context_blurb:
Two small organs that textbooks had shrugged off turned out to run the body's targeted defences. One is the thymus, a lump behind the breastbone that shrinks as you grow. The other is the bursa, a small pouch near a bird's tail. One was cracked by a classroom accident, the other by careful surgery on mice.

In 1955 at Ohio State, the poultry student Bruce Glick cut the bursa out of young chicks and saw nothing wrong. Then a fellow student borrowed his birds for a routine class demonstration, vaccinating them against a Salmonella germ. The birds without a bursa raised no antibodies, and most died: the failed demonstration had shown that the bursa is needed for making antibodies. Antibody-making cells are still called B cells after that bursa, though mammals have none. In humans, B cells finish maturing in the bone marrow.

In 1961 the Australian-born Jacques Miller, then a PhD student in London, removed the thymus from newborn mice. They never produced T cells and soon succumbed to infection. Miller is now honoured as the last scientist alive who discovered the purpose of a human organ. His mice also predicted that any baby lacking a thymus should be gravely short of T cells, and DiGeorge syndrome bears it out: in about one case in a hundred the child has no thymus at all and needs a thymus transplant.

millikans-oil-drops-and-the-slow-crawl-t.context_blurb:
Is electric charge smooth, like water, or does it come in lumps? Robert Millikan answered that at the University of Chicago between 1909 and 1913 by watching single drops of oil float in an electric field. His result won a Nobel Prize, and the story after it shows how even a good measurement can quietly steer the ones that follow.

Before Millikan, H. A. Wilson and J. J. Thomson had used clouds of water drops, but water evaporates as you watch it, so each drop kept changing its mass. Millikan and his student Harvey Fletcher used oil, which barely evaporates. They sprayed a mist between two metal plates, and each tiny drop picked up a charge. Watching one through a microscope, Millikan adjusted the plates' voltage until the electric pull upward exactly balanced the drop's weight and it hung motionless. That voltage gave him the drop's charge.

He measured hundreds of drops. The charges were never just anything: each was a whole-number multiple of a single basic amount, never one and a half of it. Charge comes in lumps, and the lump is the charge of one electron.

His 1913 value was about 0.6 percent too low. Richard Feynman, in his 1974 Caltech address "Cargo Cult Science", traced the error to one input, the viscosity of air, which is used to turn a drop's falling speed into its size. Feynman's sharper point came from the history. Later measurements did not jump to the true value; they crept up from Millikan's number in small steps over the years. A researcher who got a much higher number hunted for faults in his own apparatus, and stopped hunting once he landed near Millikan's. To guard against that pull, big physics teams now use blind analysis: they hide the key region of data, or add a secret offset, until the method is locked, and only then reveal the true result.

Not everyone agreed with Millikan. From 1910 Felix Ehrenhaft in Vienna insisted he saw charges smaller than an electron's. Everyone else's drops kept giving the same lump, but physics did later find fractional charges, on quarks, which are trapped inside protons and neutrons.

Millikan's other prize-winning work shows a scientist beaten by his own data. From 1912 to 1915 he set out to disprove Einstein's light-quantum equation for the photoelectric effect, and ended up confirming it precisely, fixing Planck's constant to within a percent.

There is a shadow on the credit. In a memoir he asked to be held back until after he died, Fletcher wrote that Millikan kept the main 1913 paper under his own name alone, pointing to a Chicago rule that a doctoral thesis needed a single author.

molina-rowland-and-the-hole-over-halley-.context_blurb:
The ozone layer, a thin veil of gas high in the stratosphere, blocks much of the Sun's harshest ultraviolet light. In the 1970s and 1980s chemists showed that a family of supposedly harmless factory gases was eating it, and then measured the damage over Antarctica. Few warnings in science have been tested so directly or answered so fast.

The gases were chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, the coolants of refrigerators and the propellants of aerosol cans. Their champion was Thomas Midgley Jr., the chemist who had already given the world leaded petrol. In 1930, to prove his new refrigerant Freon was safe, he breathed in a lungful before the American Chemical Society and blew it out over a candle, putting out the flame.

That inertness was the trouble. Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland asked in 1974 where CFCs end up. Nothing near the ground breaks them down, so they drift intact into the stratosphere, where the Sun's ultraviolet light finally splits them and sets chlorine atoms loose. Each chlorine atom acts as a catalyst, destroying ozone without being used up, so a single one can wreck around 100,000 ozone molecules before it is finally removed. The chairman of DuPont, the biggest seller of CFCs, dismissed the theory publicly as science fiction, a load of rubbish and utter nonsense. Molina and Rowland built on Paul Crutzen, who in 1970 had shown that nitrogen oxides, made from nitrous oxide, eat ozone in the same catalytic way; all three shared the 1995 chemistry Nobel.

Then came the measurement. Since the 1950s a British station at Halley Bay on the Antarctic coast had tracked ozone with a hand-calibrated ground instrument, and its October readings kept falling. In 1985 Farman and two colleagues reported in Nature that each southern spring the ozone column over Antarctica was dropping by up to 70 percent. Two years later nations signed the Montreal Protocol to freeze and then halve CFC production, and it remains the only UN environmental treaty that every member state has ratified. Atmospheric chlorine peaked in the late 1990s and has fallen since.

NASA's satellite might have seen the hole first. The story that its software threw the low readings away is a myth: a 1993 NASA report showed that values below 180 Dobson units were flagged as suspected sensor errors, set aside for a person to check later. Other data showed normal ozone, so the team suspected a faulty sensor. Reprocessed, the archive had held the hole all along. A filter built around what you expect can hide what you do not.

The hole also puzzled chemists, because the 1974 chemistry predicted slow global thinning, not a deep hole in one place. In 1986 Susan Solomon led an expedition to Antarctica and proposed that the key reactions were happening on the surfaces of the ice crystals that make up polar stratospheric clouds, which form only in the extreme cold of the polar winter. There, harmless chlorine compounds turn into active chlorine that waits for the spring sun and then strikes all at once. Late in 1987, instruments built by James Anderson's team flew into the polar vortex aboard NASA's ER-2, a research version of the U-2 spy plane. Their famous plot showed chlorine monoxide soaring at exactly the place and time that ozone collapsed: the smoking gun.

moseley-counts-the-charges-and-re-orders.context_blurb:
Henry Moseley, a young English physicist, spent barely two years on one experiment and found in it the true ordering rule of the periodic table. Before him the table was sorted by atomic weight, with awkward exceptions; after him it was sorted by a simple count. He was killed in the First World War at twenty-seven.

In 1913 Moseley loaded a vacuum tube with one pure metal at a time and fired a beam of electrons at each, knocking out electrons deep inside its atoms. As other electrons fell into the gaps, each element gave off X-rays of its own frequency, which he caught on photographic film. Element by element, the frequencies climbed in a perfectly regular staircase, one step per element. In 1914 he argued that the whole number on each step was a real count: the number of positive charges in the atom's nucleus, what we now call the atomic number.

That cleared up Mendeleev's puzzles. Mendeleev's chemistry had placed tellurium ahead of iodine and cobalt ahead of nickel, against the scales. Moseley showed the order was right: tellurium carries one fewer charge in its nucleus than iodine, and cobalt one fewer than nickel, even though each is the heavier of its pair, because the extra weight is neutrons.

Because the staircase allowed no missing steps, Moseley could point at the gaps. He named four elements that had to exist but had not been found, numbers 43, 61, 72 and 75, later filled by technetium, promethium, hafnium and rhenium. The table stopped being a matter of judgement and became a matter of counting.

Moseley joined the British Army as a volunteer when war came, and on 10 August 1915 a Turkish sniper shot him dead at Gallipoli. Robert Millikan called his death one of the war's heaviest costs to science. He never received a Nobel Prize, because the prize is never given to someone who has died.

n-rays-and-the-anatomy-of-pathological-s.context_blurb:
In 1903 René Blondlot, a respected physicist at the University of Nancy in France, claimed to have discovered a fresh type of radiation and named it the N-ray, after his city. For three years it was a busy, respectable field of physics. Then a single visitor showed that the rays existed only in the minds of the people looking for them.

Blondlot said N-rays poured out of iron, out of wood, even out of the human brain. To detect them, an observer sat in a dark room watching a tiny spark or a faint strip of glowing paint and judged by eye whether it brightened. The fatal flaw was that the observer always knew which moments were meant to be the "on" ones, so expectation itself became the instrument. Even so, other labs confirmed the rays, and about 120 scientists published some 300 papers on them.

Robert W. Wood, an American physicist, came to Nancy in 1904 to watch a demonstration. In the dark he quietly pocketed the aluminium prism that was supposed to spread the rays into a spectrum, and the demonstrator went on reading off the same spectrum as before. Wood also swapped an ordinary chunk of wood for a steel file said to give off the rays. Wood, by Blondlot's own list, gave off none, yet the readings kept coming. Wood's letter to Nature showed the rays were imaginary: they had never existed at all.

The French Academy of Sciences did not abandon its own. In December 1904, months after Wood's letter, it still handed Blondlot its Prix Leconte, worth 50,000 francs, but quietly reworded the citation to honour his work as a whole instead of the rays. Blondlot kept his chair and reportedly believed in N-rays to the end.

In 1953 the chemist Irving Langmuir gave the pattern a name, pathological science: effects that stay at the edge of detection, never grow when the cause is strengthened, and survive every failed test with a fresh excuse. Polywater fits it. For a decade chemists chased polywater, a strange variety of water said to freeze at minus 40 and boil at 150 degrees, until in 1971 the Bell Labs chemist Denis Rousseau played a game of handball, collected his own sweat, and showed that its infrared spectrum matched polywater's. The "new water" was ordinary water contaminated with salts.

Cold fusion followed the same arc. In March 1989 Stanley Pons and Martin Fleischmann, chemists in Utah, claimed fusion in a tabletop jar of heavy water, and they announced it at a press conference, before any paper had gone to peer review. Laboratories around the world could not reproduce the excess heat.

natural-immunity-the-oldest-measured-fac.context_blurb:
Surviving an infection usually leaves you protected against that same disease, often for life. It is one of the oldest measured facts in medicine, first written down some 2,400 years ago and tested again and again since, from a measles epidemic in the North Atlantic to the COVID-19 pandemic. Its price can be high, and its limits are as real as its strength.

In 430 BC plague struck Athens. The historian Thucydides caught it and lived, and he noticed who nursed the dying without fear: people who had already had the disease and recovered, because, he wrote, nobody caught it twice, at least not fatally. He also recorded a mistake. In the joy of survival, the recovered half-believed they would never fall sick of anything again, a true finding stretched into a false one.

In 1846 measles reached the Faroe Islands after sixty-five years away and sickened about 6,000 of some 7,800 islanders. Denmark sent a 25-year-old doctor, Peter Ludvig Panum, to investigate. He went looking for those it had spared and found them among the elderly, who had caught measles in their youth, during the epidemic of 1781. Was it old age that protected them, or the earlier illness? Panum checked the old people whom the 1781 epidemic had passed by, and without exception they fell ill this time. Age did nothing; having had the disease did everything.

Remote villages let him time the disease, since a household often met it on one known day, and he pinned the gap from exposure to rash at about two weeks. At one farmhouse the churchwarden's daughter had just recovered while nine others felt fine. Panum counted forward from her rash and marked the day the rest of the house would fall ill, and he was right so often that he won a reputation for prophecy.

The immunity was not free. About 170 islanders died, and very unevenly: about three in a thousand of the children between one and nine, but nearly three in ten of the babies under a year old.

Why does it last? The first time a germ invades, the body takes most of a week to answer with antibody, and that first batch grips loosely. The second time, antibody arrives within one to three days, grips hard, and comes in a hundred to a thousand times the amount, so the fight is over before you feel ill. Years later some antibody factories, the long-lived plasma cells, are still at work, because they settled into survival niches in the bone marrow and stayed there for decades. In 2008 researchers drew blood from 32 people aged 91 to 101, small children when the 1918 flu struck. Cells from some of them still made antibody that protected mice from a lethal dose of the 1918 strain, ninety years on.

Measles protects for life while flu returns each winter because of the viruses, not the body: measles hardly changes as it copies itself, so a survivor's memory still recognises it half a century later, while flu reshapes its surface every year. Breadth matters too. COVID-19 shots built on mRNA or protein subunits presented just one part of the virus, its spike. People who caught the virus met all of it, and kept T-cell memory aimed at the nucleocapsid, a protein wrapped round the virus's genetic material, which changes far less between variants.

Much public messaging in 2020 and 2021 treated prior infection as if it could not be counted, yet it was measured. California and New York tracked case rates through 2021 by vaccination and past infection, and the CDC reported the results in January 2022. Before Delta, people vaccinated without prior infection had the lower rate. By early October the order had flipped, and survivors of an earlier infection had the lower rate. A 2023 Lancet review of 65 studies found reinfection protection had slipped to roughly one third after forty weeks, while protection against severe disease still stood near ninety percent. Quoting only one half, in either direction, turns a measurement into a slogan.

Measles carries a hidden cost. Michael Mina and colleagues tested the blood of 77 unvaccinated children against thousands of germs before and after measles, and found the illness had wiped out between 11 and 73 percent of the antibodies they already carried against other diseases.
