natural-selection-an-algorithm-with-no-f.context_blurb:
Natural selection is the process Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace discovered: more young are born than can survive, they vary, and the variation is inherited, so whatever helps gets passed on. Nothing plans it and nothing aims at a goal. That is why its results can be brilliant and clumsy at once, and why it can be tested.

Darwin opened On the Origin of Species with pigeons. Breeders had produced fantails with forty tail feathers, pouters with swollen crops and tumblers with stubby beaks, yet all of them descended from one wild bird, the rock pigeon. Darwin gathered his own evidence. He bought and bred every kind he could get, and became a member of two London pigeon clubs.

The pressure behind selection is arithmetic. Darwin chose the elephant, the slowest-breeding animal of all, and reckoned that if every calf of a single pair survived and bred, after 500 years there would be about fifteen million elephants. Most young must die. He had seen the point in September 1838, reading Thomas Malthus's argument that human numbers outrun food. Darwin applied it to all life and saw in a flash that in such a struggle any inherited variation that helped even slightly would tend to be preserved, and harmful ones destroyed.

He sat on the idea for twenty years. Then Alfred Russel Wallace, collecting in the Malay Archipelago, sent him the same idea worked out on his own. On 1 July 1858 the Linnean Society heard both men's papers, read aloud one after the other. The Origin followed in November 1859.

The rival theory, from Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, held that changes an animal acquires during its life are inherited. August Weismann tested it bluntly: he cut the tails off white mice for five generations, and every one of the 901 young grew a full, normal tail.

Selection can be watched. Around Manchester, factory soot blackened tree bark, and the peppered moth's black form rose to 95 percent of moths counted by 1898, then fell below one percent after the air was cleaned. No moth ever changed colour: both forms were there all along, and birds ate whichever stood out against the bark. On the Galápagos island of Daphne Major the biologists Rosemary and Peter Grant have weighed and measured finches every year since 1973. A drought in 1976-77 left only big, hard seeds, and the following generation had beaks about five percent deeper. When drought returned in 2003 the seed supply was different, and beaks grew shallower, the opposite way.

Fitness in biology means descendants, not strength. A stag that wins every fight for forty years but sires no young has a fitness of zero, while a rival beaten in every contest who raises nine sons is the fitter. The phrase "survival of the fittest" was Herbert Spencer's, and Darwin adopted it only later. The peacock's tail troubled Darwin badly, since so big a train makes a bird easier to catch. His answer, published in 1871, was a second mechanism, sexual selection, driven by competition for mates rather than survival.

Having no foresight shows in our bodies. The recurrent laryngeal nerve, which works the voice box, does not run straight there. It travels down into the chest, loops under the arch of the aorta, and climbs back up to the larynx; in a giraffe the detour runs for metres. In fish-like ancestors the nerve took a short, straight path to the gills, passing the heart. As necks evolved and lengthened, the blood vessel it hooks beneath was pulled back into the chest, and the nerve was dragged along with it. A designer would have rerouted the wire; selection can only edit what it inherits.

Not every change is adaptive. Genetic drift is change by sampling luck, strongest in small populations: a pair of Amish settlers who arrived in Pennsylvania in 1744 passed a rare syndrome to their descendants that has never helped any of them. In 1968 Motoo Kimura argued that most genetic change that spreads through a species is drift acting on mutations that make no difference either way.

The theory can also be killed. Descent with modification forbids certain fossils: a rabbit's skeleton lying in rock laid down before any shelled animal lived would wreck it, because no ancestor of any mammal existed yet. After more than 150 years of digging, nobody has found one.

neil-fergusons-numbers-checked.context_blurb:
Neil Ferguson, an epidemiologist at Imperial College London, leads one of the world's most influential teams of disease modellers. Their computer models have shaped government decisions on mad cow disease, foot-and-mouth, bird flu, swine flu and COVID-19. Because Ferguson published his numbers with his name and a date on them, anyone can check them against what happened.

On 16 March 2020 his team released Report 9, projecting about 510,000 British and 2.2 million American deaths in a scenario with no action at all. Governments around the world soon ordered lockdowns. In Britain, Prime Minister Boris Johnson went on television on 23 March and announced a national lockdown, telling people to stay at home. Ferguson later told the COVID Inquiry that the report's scenarios were widely reported as forecasts.

The model used one infection fatality rate for the whole population, 0.9 percent. Later blood surveys showed that the real risk climbed steeply with age, from almost nothing in the young to several percent in the very old, so a single average hid the factor that mattered most.

Earlier projections show a pattern. In 2002 Ferguson's group put the future British death toll from variant CJD, the disease people caught from mad cows, anywhere from 50 to 50,000; by 2016 the total had settled at 178. In 2005 Ferguson warned that bird flu, H5N1, could kill some 200 million people if it learned to spread easily between humans. It never did, and the WHO's count of confirmed human deaths from 2003 to 2024 came to about 500 worldwide. In the summer of 2009 Sir Liam Donaldson, England's top doctor, told the press that swine flu might claim 65,000 British lives that winter, a figure from planning that Imperial was part of; the real toll across the UK was 457. Each big number was the top of a range or a worst case resting on a condition, and the modellers said so. The trouble came when the upper bound was reported as the number.

The code behind Report 9 came under scrutiny too. When it went public on GitHub in May 2020, the famous game programmer John Carmack, who had helped tidy it, described one sprawling file with parts that looked machine-translated from Fortran: messy and hard to read, though it held up better under his analysis tools than much modern code. In June 2020 Stephen Eglen at Cambridge reproduced the report's key findings. The code was rough, and its headline result held up.

The record goes back further. During Britain's 2001 epidemic of foot-and-mouth disease, Imperial's models backed a rule of culling the animals on farms next to any infected one, and more than six million cattle and sheep were killed. At the COVID Inquiry Ferguson himself drew the line worth remembering: fitting a model to past data and forecasting the future are different jobs. A forecast counts as science only when someone writes the number down, dates it, and comes back to check.

neptune-found-on-paper.context_blurb:
Neptune is the only planet found by mathematics before anyone knew where to look. In 1846 Urbain Le Verrier, a mathematician in Paris, worked out where an unseen world must be from the way it tugged on Uranus, and astronomers in Berlin found it on their first night of searching. The full story mixes brilliant calculation, missed chances and a measure of luck.

In September 1846 Le Verrier sent precise directions to Johann Galle in Berlin: aim at longitude 326 degrees in the constellation Aquarius, where a faint planet showing a small disc should lie within a degree. Galle asked his director, Johann Franz Encke, for time on the big telescope. Encke shrugged that they might as well oblige the gentleman in Paris, and spent the evening away; 23 September was his birthday. Galle's student Heinrich d'Arrest pulled from a drawer a star chart of exactly that region, so new that copies had not yet gone out in the post to other observatories, so anything missing from it would stand out at once. Galle called out star positions from the eyepiece while d'Arrest checked the chart. Barely half an hour into the search, d'Arrest cried out that one star was not on the map: it was the planet itself, within a degree of the predicted place.

Seventeen days later William Lassell, an English brewer who had ground the mirror for his own large telescope, turned it on the new planet and found a large moon, Triton, circling it every six days. A moon's orbit gives a planet's mass, so Triton let astronomers weigh Neptune.

The hunt began with Uranus. In 1821 Alexis Bouvard published tables predicting its position, and within a few years it had strayed from them, running ahead until about 1822 and then falling behind. Bouvard printed the failure honestly and wondered whether some unseen cause was pulling on the planet. The pull's strength could be worked out, but not its source, because a modest planet nearby and a massive one far away would disturb Uranus almost alike. Le Verrier in Paris and John Couch Adams in Cambridge both broke the deadlock the same way, by placing the new planet where Bode's rule, a popular pattern in planetary distances, said the next world should be. Neptune turned out not to fit Bode's rule at all.

Adams had sent his own predicted position to the Astronomer Royal, George Airy, in 1845. Airy replied with one technical question: would the same planet also explain the errors in Uranus's distance from the Sun? It was a real test, built to tell a hidden planet from a flaw in the law of gravity, but Adams felt dismissed and let the letter lie. From July 1846 James Challis at Cambridge swept the sky with Adams's numbers in hand, recording thousands of star positions. Neptune appeared in his logs twice in August, but he never compared one night's positions with another's to see which point had moved.

Neptune had been seen long before. In May 1795 Joseph Jérôme Lalande's team at the Paris Observatory measured it on the 8th and again on the 10th and got two different positions. They discarded the first reading as an error and printed only the second, deleting the very evidence that it moved. Galileo had drawn it near Jupiter on 28 December 1612 and listed it as a fixed star. That mistake was nearly unavoidable: Neptune was at the turning point of its loop, reversing direction, and so barely moving against the stars.

Luck rode along with the mathematics. Le Verrier's planet orbited about 36 times as far out as Earth, and Adams's about 37, but the real Neptune circles at about 30. Their wrong orbits still pointed the right way because, over the short stretch of sky covered by the observations, the wrong path ran close to the true one. In 1847 the American mathematician Benjamin Peirce told his academy in Boston that the analysis had been aimed at a different planet from the one Galle found, and that the find was a happy accident. Astronomers still argue over how far Peirce was right.

newtons-plague-years-and-the-principia.context_blurb:
In 1665 plague closed Cambridge University and sent a 22-year-old Isaac Newton home. In about eighteen months away from college he began his calculus, split sunlight with a prism and started thinking about gravity. Twenty years later that thinking became the Principia, the book that put the heavens and the Earth under one law.

Home was Woolsthorpe Manor, the family farm in Lincolnshire, where he spent most of 1665 and 1666, later calling them the prime of his age for invention. The famous apple belongs there too. Newton told the story himself at 83, over tea under apple trees in Kensington in 1726, and William Stukeley wrote it down: an apple had fallen to the ground while Newton sat thinking, and he wondered why it always dropped straight toward the Earth's centre. No early account has it striking his head. The tree, a Flower of Kent, a sour green variety meant for cooking, still grows at Woolsthorpe: a storm blew it over in 1816, but its trunk stayed largely whole, put down new roots where it lay and kept growing. You can go and stand beside it.

There he compared two pulls, the one that keeps the Moon on its track and the one that drops a stone in a field. They answered pretty nearly, he wrote later: near enough to be encouraging, though not exact. The fault lay in one number, the size of the Earth: he had used the sailors' rough figure of 60 miles to a degree of latitude, when the truth is nearer 69.

The same years gave him his work on light. Others had thrown prism colours on a wall and said the glass tinted the light. Newton darkened a room, let a thin beam through a hole in the shutter, and then took the step that made a proof: he isolated one colour of the spread and sent it through a second prism. It stayed the same colour, so the prism was sorting white light, not staining it.

Edmond Halley came to Cambridge in August 1684 with a question: what path would a planet follow under a pull that weakens with the square of the distance? Newton said at once that it would be an ellipse, and when Halley asked how he knew, he answered that he had calculated it, then could not find the paper. He promised to redo the work, and it grew into the Principia. When the Royal Society ordered the book printed in 1686 it had no money, having spent its budget on a book about fish that nobody bought, so Halley covered the printing costs himself.

The Principia's picture of an orbit needs no mathematics. Imagine a cannon on a mountain so tall it rises above the air. Fired gently, the ball curves down nearby; fired harder, it lands farther off; fired hard enough, it keeps falling but keeps missing the ground, because the Earth curves away beneath it as fast as it drops. That is an orbit, and it is why the Moon never comes down on our heads.

Before Newton, learned Europe split the world in two: below the Moon's orbit things fell, rusted and decayed, while above it the heavens wheeled forever by other rules. The Principia put the falling apple, the Moon, the tides and the comets under one law. It had a serious rival. Most European scientists followed René Descartes, who in 1644 pictured the planets carried round the Sun by an invisible whirling fluid, like leaves swept along in a stream. Newton spent a whole section of the Principia showing that such whirlpools could not fit Kepler's laws.

Robert Hooke claimed credit. He had written to Newton in 1680 that attraction drops with the square of the distance, and when the Principia arrived he accused Newton of taking the idea. Yet in the same breath Hooke granted that the proof that the planets' curved paths follow from one law of attraction was Newton's own. Hooke had the rule; Newton had shown that the rule produces the sky we see.

Newton was stranger than the textbook hero. John Maynard Keynes, the economist, bought a hoard of his unpublished papers at a 1936 auction, and a large part concerns alchemy, the attempt to transmute metals and find the philosopher's stone; Indiana University has put 131 such manuscripts online. Keynes called him not the first of the age of reason but the last of the magicians.

newtons-prism-and-the-experimentum-cruci.context_blurb:
In 1666, with Cambridge shut by plague, the young Isaac Newton turned a darkened room at his family's farmhouse into a laboratory for light. With a few prisms and boards he showed that white sunlight is a mixture of colours, and his tests remain a model of how to try to break your own idea.

He let a thin sunbeam through a small hole in his window shutter and onto a prism. The rules of refraction said the patch on the far wall should be round, but it came out as an oblong smear about five times longer than it was broad. He measured that surprise instead of just admiring it. The accepted story said that white light was pure and simple, and that glass stained colour into it. Newton suspected the opposite: white light was already a mixture, and the prism only sorted it.

To rule out tricks of bad glass, he built what he called his experimentum crucis, the crucial experiment. He placed two boards, each with a small hole, so that out of the whole spread of colours only a single one could pass through both and reach a second prism. That lone colour came out of the second prism unchanged and would not split any further; in his word, it kept its colour obstinately. Then he ran the test backwards. A lens gathered the whole spread and merged it into white again, but when he held back one colour before it reached the lens, the spot turned coloured instead of white.

Prism colours were not new. Descartes had studied them, and in 1648 Jan Marek Marci reported that a separated colour is not changed by bending it again. What Newton added was measurement: each colour bends by its own fixed amount, and white light is the mixture of them all.

The name experimentum crucis came from Francis Bacon and Robert Hooke, and Newton used the experiment against Hooke's own theory, set out in his 1665 Micrographia, that light is a pulse spreading through an ether filling all space. When Newton's 1672 letter on colour appeared, Hooke replied that he had done such experiments years earlier and that they fitted his account just as well. Stung, Newton shelved his book on light for more than thirty years. Opticks appeared only in 1704, after Hooke had died.

His colour work also persuaded Newton that a lens would always blur its image with coloured fringes, so he built a telescope with a curved metal mirror instead. Barely six inches long, it magnified about 35 times, and through it he saw the crescent of Venus and the four moons of Jupiter. It was shown to the Royal Society and to King Charles II. Newton was wrong about lenses, though. Chester Moore Hall, a lawyer who ground lenses in his spare time, combined a lens of one kind of glass with a lens of another, so that their colour errors cancelled, and tried to keep the trick secret.

Newton also asked whether colour lives in the light or in the eye, and tested it in a way no one should ever copy: he pushed a bodkin, a long blunt needle, into the gap behind his own eyeball and pressed on it, recording the coloured circles that appeared.

His conclusion that colour is carried by the light can be tested on a street at night. An old orange sodium lamp gives out light of almost a single wavelength, so a bright red car parked under one photographs flat black: there is no red in the light for the paint to send back.

Newton named seven colours in the rainbow. He first wrote down six, then slipped in indigo, between blue and violet, so that the colours would match the seven notes of a musical scale. The spectrum itself is seamless; the names are human labels laid over it.

The poet Goethe spent twenty years attacking Newton, arguing that colour is born where light meets dark. Mixing lights is where his scheme fails: blue paint and yellow paint make green, but a yellow lamp and a blue one aimed at one white wall overlap as white, like ordinary daylight. You can check it with two torches and coloured cellophane.

nightingales-rose-diagram.context_blurb:
Florence Nightingale is remembered as the lady with the lamp, but her sharpest weapon was a chart. In charge of the army's hospital at Scutari, in Turkey, during the Crimean War of the 1850s, she watched soldiers die of filth and infection. Afterwards she used numbers and pictures to force the government to change how it cared for its men.

The numbers were stark. Of roughly 18,000 Britons who died in the war, some 16,000 were killed by preventable disease such as typhus, cholera and dysentery, not from Russian weapons. In 1858 she published a picture made for readers not used to figures: a coloured circle split into twelve wedges, one for each month, with blue for disease, red for wounds and black for other causes. The blue dwarfed everything.

Her chart has one honest flaw. Each wedge kept the same angle and was stretched outward by the death count, but a wedge's area grows with the square of its length, so the worst months look far worse than they were. Redraw the same counts as a bar chart on graph paper and the winter spike shrinks to its true size.

Her partner in the arithmetic was William Farr of the General Register Office, who had designed the first proper scheme for classifying why Britons died. Together they used the figures to press for better hygiene and sanitation in hospitals. She turned the lesson on peacetime Britain too, showing that soldiers in barracks at home were dying almost twice as fast as civilians, and the government set up a Royal Commission on the Health of the Army, chaired by Sidney Herbert, which brought new building codes, an army medical school and a statistics office.

The strange part is her theory. Nightingale distrusted contagion and blamed disease on bad air given off by filth and rot, the old miasma idea. Her ventilation, drainage and scrubbing worked anyway, because they also attacked the germs she did not believe in. She trusted the numbers more than the explanation.

nullius-in-verba-take-nobodys-word-for-i.context_blurb:
The Royal Society of London, founded in November 1660 after a lecture by Christopher Wren at Gresham College, is the oldest scientific society still running. Its motto, three Latin words on its coat of arms, sums up the method that made modern science: Nullius in verba. It is a rule against resting any claim on an authority's say-so.

In plain English the motto tells you to take nobody's word, whoever is speaking, and to check for yourself. The words come from the Roman poet Horace, who wrote in his Epistles that he was sworn to follow no teacher's words, and the Fellows clipped the phrase from that line. That familiar English version is not a translation of Horace. It is the Society's own idiomatic gloss on the Latin, which literally means "on the word of no one".

In the 1660s the Fellows explained the choice: they meant to stand firm against the rule of authority and to settle every claim by an appeal to facts determined by experiment. That was roughly three and a half centuries before anyone was told to trust the science.

In 1974 the physicist Richard Feynman turned the motto inward. In his commencement speech at Caltech he said the first principle is that you must not fool yourself, because you are the easiest person of all to fool. In the same speech he described South Pacific islanders who, after the Second World War, built runways, lit fires and sat a man in a hut wearing wooden headphones, waiting for cargo planes that never came. He gave the name cargo cult science to research that copies the outward form of science while skipping the honest effort to find out whether it is wrong.

A test anyone can carry: ask what evidence would change the speaker's mind. A claim that comes with a way to check it is doing science; a claim that comes with a demand for deference is doing something else.

oersteds-needle-and-the-accident-that-wa.context_blurb:
In April 1820, in Copenhagen, the Danish physicist Hans Christian Ørsted made a compass needle swing by passing an electric current through a nearby wire. It was the first proof that electricity and magnetism are linked, the seed of every motor and generator. The popular story calls it a lucky accident; Ørsted's own account says otherwise.

He had been hunting the link for years, driven by philosophy. His 1799 doctoral thesis held no experiments at all; it was about Immanuel Kant's metaphysics, the foundations natural science rests on, and it left him sure that all the forces of nature spring from one power.

For an evening lecture in April 1820 the test stood ready on the bench, but with no chance to rehearse, Ørsted planned to skip it and save the test for another day. During the lecture he changed his mind and ran it in front of the class. The needle, shut in a box, was disturbed, but the effect was so feeble that the audience barely reacted. Then, remembering how others had fooled themselves on this very question, he left the experiment untouched for three months.

In July he returned with a far stronger battery, twenty copper troughs, and the effect became impossible to miss. A wire held above the needle swung one pole west, while the same wire beneath it, current flowing the same way, swung that pole east, the opposite way. Moved from the needle's east side to its west side, the wire turned the same pole the same way from both, which ruled out a simple attraction between wire and needle. The force must run in circles around the wire. It passed through glass, metal, wood and stone, and still moved a needle shut inside a brass box full of water. He named whatever filled the space around the wire the conflict of electricity, and his pamphlet's Latin title is built around it.

Before printing a word, he did every experiment again with six invited men watching, among them professors and a chemist, and named them in print. The pamphlet, dated 21 July 1820, went by post to scientists across Europe.

When François Arago reported it to the Académie des Sciences in Paris on 4 September, the room met it with disbelief. A week later Arago stopped arguing and performed the experiment himself in front of the members. On 25 September André-Marie Ampère went further, with no magnet anywhere: two live wires lying side by side pulled toward each other when their currents ran the same way, and pushed apart when they ran opposite.

You can repeat it tonight. With a flat compass and a wire laid along the needle, a brief contact with an AA battery, with a resistor in the circuit, makes the needle jump. Lay the wire across the needle instead, east to west, and the needle stays put, because the field circles the wire. Keep the contact short, since the wire gets hot.

Why had nobody found it in the two decades after Volta's first battery? Ørsted noted that celebrated natural philosophers had tried years before and failed because they never closed the circuit, and an open circuit carries no current. Ampère named a deeper block: Coulomb's hypothesis about the nature of magnetism, which everyone had treated as a fact, ruled out any link with electricity, so the test seemed pointless.

ohm-and-the-book-called-a-web-of-naked-f.context_blurb:
Georg Simon Ohm was a schoolteacher in Cologne who, in the 1820s, found the simple rule linking the electrical push of a voltage to the current it drives through a wire. Germany's leading physicists mocked his book, and he waited years for the recognition his name now carries.

Teaching mathematics and physics at the Jesuit school in Cologne, Ohm had no laboratory budget, so he made his own apparatus and even drew his own wire. His first readings would not settle. The fault was in his power source, a voltaic pile, Volta's stack of copper and zinc discs, whose output sagged steadily as it ran. His friend Johann Christian Poggendorff suggested a steadier source: the pairing of bismuth and copper that Thomas Seebeck had shown drives a current when its two joints differ in temperature. Ohm kept one joint in boiling water and the other in melting ice, so the source held as steady as those two temperatures.

For the mathematics he borrowed from Joseph Fourier, who had worked out how heat flows along a metal bar: a temperature difference drives the heat, and the bar's length resists it. Ohm swapped voltage for temperature and current for heat. His 1827 book said current rises with voltage and falls with resistance, so a wire twice as long carries half the current. German critics, who thought mathematics had no place in describing electricity, sneered at it, and their phrase for the book, "web of naked fancies", became famous. Ohm resigned his post and spent years tutoring before the Royal Society gave him its Copley Medal in 1841.

His rule is not a law of nature in the way gravity is. It holds cleanly for a length of ordinary copper wire kept at a steady temperature, but it fails for many other things; a glowing lamp filament, for one, resists more and more as it heats. Knowing where a rule breaks is knowing more than the rule.

oklo-the-reactor-that-ran-itself-for-a-f.context_blurb:
In 1972 a routine check at a French uranium plant found ore from the Oklo mine in Gabon, in West Africa, with too little of the fissile isotope uranium-235. Investigators suspected theft. The truth was stranger: some 1,700 million years earlier, parts of that ore body had worked as natural nuclear reactors, with groundwater slowing the neutrons and no one there at all.

It could not happen today because the fuel has changed. Uranium-235 decays faster than uranium-238, so the further back you go, the richer natural uranium was in it. Back then it was about 3 percent uranium-235, the same level a modern power reactor burns; today it is about 0.7 percent.

The rock still carries the reactors' fingerprints. In ordinary ruthenium, about one atom in eight is ruthenium-99, but in the Oklo zones the share runs 27 to 30 percent. The surplus came from technetium-99, a typical product of fission, which decayed into ruthenium-99.

Modellers even recovered the reactors' rhythm: about half an hour on and two and a half hours off, as the water boiled away and seeped back, kept up for hundreds of thousands of years. The record is the xenon locked inside aluminium phosphate crystals in the old reactor zones, because some xenon escaped while a reactor ran hot and other xenon arrived later and was frozen in.

one-atom-four-bonds-four-worlds.context_blurb:
A diamond and a pencil's grey core look like opposites: one is the hardest natural mineral, the other smears on your thumb. Yet both are pure carbon and nothing else. The whole difference lies in how each atom bonds to its neighbours, and chemists have spent 250 years proving it, measuring it and finding new forms.

Pencils have never held any lead. In the 1560s miners at Borrowdale in Cumbria dug out a soft black mineral and called it plumbago, lead ore, which is why many languages still speak of a "lead pen". It was graphite, named in 1789 from the Greek for "to write". When the pure Borrowdale stock ran short, Nicolas-Jacques Conté in 1795 mixed powdered graphite with clay, shaped it into rods and fired them in a kiln, and pencil cores are still made that way, with the clay share setting the hardness.

In diamond, each carbon atom grips four neighbours at the corners of a tetrahedron, and the pattern repeats in every direction, a rigid three-dimensional cage with no easy plane to slide along. In graphite each atom bonds to only three, laying the atoms out in flat honeycomb sheets stacked loosely like pages. Drag a pencil across paper and whole sheets of atoms slide off intact and stay behind on the page.

Diamond is hard but not indestructible. Heated past about 800 °C, it catches fire and burns away with no ash at all, because burning carbon leaves only gas. In 1773 Antoine Lavoisier used a giant burning lens to set a diamond alight inside a sealed glass jar, then weighed the whole apparatus: it weighed exactly what it had before, because the diamond had become a gas, carbon dioxide, still trapped inside. In 1797 Smithson Tennant showed what diamond is. He burned powdered diamond with nitre, a salt that releases oxygen, and measured the gas. That alone proved nothing, so he repeated the whole procedure with an equal weight of charcoal, and the two gave exactly the same amount of the same gas. A comparison, not a single result, settled it.

New forms kept appearing. In 1985 the Sussex chemist Harold Kroto travelled to Rice University in Texas, chasing long carbon chains that radio astronomers had found around ageing red giant stars, in their outer atmospheres. With Richard Smalley and Robert Curl he blasted graphite with a laser to copy that star chemistry, and the machine kept producing 60 carbon atoms joined in one hollow cage of hexagons and pentagons, shaped like a football. They named it buckminsterfullerene.

In 2004 at Manchester, Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov peeled graphene, a layer of carbon just one atom deep, off a block of graphite using nothing more than sticky tape, stuck down and peeled away over and over. It won them a Nobel Prize in 2010. No material yet tested is stronger than graphene: James Hone, who helped measure it, said that to punch through a sheet of graphene as thick as plastic food wrap you would need the weight of an elephant perched on the tip of a pencil.

Test graphite's electricity at home. Draw a thick, dark pencil line, clip a coin cell to one point on it and an LED to another, then slide a clip along: the LED shines, and grows fainter the farther apart the clips are, because a pencil line is a resistor that grows with its length. Graphite conducts because each atom's fourth electron roams freely across its sheet; in diamond every electron is tied into a bond.

Diamond hides more surprises. It carries heat better than any other solid, over five times better than copper, yet it has no loose electrons; the heat travels as vibrations of the whole lattice racing along its stiff bonds. Graphite is soft, but not because its bonds are weak: inside a sheet the carbons sit 0.142 nanometres apart, closer and stronger than diamond's 0.154. Its sheets slide because they cling to each other only weakly, across a much wider gap. And a diamond is not forever. At everyday conditions graphite is carbon's more stable form, so every diamond is slowly turning into it, but the change needs every bond in the lattice broken and rebuilt, a push of energy so large that the change drags on for millions or even billions of years.

one-letter-sickle-cell-from-herricks-sli.context_blurb:
Sickle-cell disease is a painful, often deadly inherited illness of the blood, common in parts of Africa, the Mediterranean and India. Over half a century, scientists traced it from a strange shape under a microscope down to a single changed letter of DNA, and then found out why evolution kept such a harmful gene so common.

James Herrick, a Chicago doctor, examined in 1910 Walter Clement Noel, a young man from Grenada studying dentistry, who was pale, breathless and suffering from leg ulcers. Under the microscope Herrick's resident, Ernest Irons, saw red cells stretched into long, curved crescents like sickles, a shape no textbook showed. The disease was named for that shape decades before anyone knew its cause.

In 1949 Linus Pauling's team at Caltech drove normal and sickle haemoglobin, the blood's oxygen-carrying protein, through a gel under an electric field, and the sickle form drifted differently because it carried a little more positive charge. Their paper called sickle-cell anaemia a molecular disease, the first illness traced to one faulty molecule.

In 1956 Vernon Ingram, working under Max Perutz at Cambridge, chopped haemoglobin into short pieces and spread them across paper, using an electric current in one direction and chemistry in the other. He called the pattern of spots a fingerprint, and the normal and sickle fingerprints matched except for one spot. Inside that one piece, in the sixth link of haemoglobin's beta chain, valine had taken the place of glutamic acid, because a single DNA letter had turned GAG into GTG.

That swap matters because glutamic acid loves water while valine is greasy. When haemoglobin has given up its oxygen, the greasy patch on one molecule sticks to the next, and the molecules stack into long, stiff fibres that bend the cell into a sickle from inside.

In 1949 J. B. S. Haldane asked why a gene that often kills children who carry two copies stays so common. Anthony Allison answered in East Africa in the 1950s: children with just one copy gained strong protection against severe falciparum malaria, so the gene thrives wherever that malaria does. It is natural selection visible in a living human population, cruel arithmetic and all.

one-shot-for-life-luxturna-and-zolgensma.context_blurb:
Gene therapy means giving a patient a working copy of a broken gene. Two of its first triumphs, Luxturna for a rare inherited blindness and Zolgensma for a deadly muscle-wasting disease of babies, use a harmless virus, the adeno-associated virus or AAV, as the delivery van. Each is given once, and why only once is part of the story.

Children whose RPE65 genes are both broken cannot properly recycle the vitamin-A molecule their retina needs to reset after each flash of light. The first thing they lose is sight in dim light, at dusk and at night; daytime vision fades later. Luxturna, approved in the United States in December 2017, carries a working RPE65 gene. A surgeon slips it in under the retina, at the rear of the eyeball, right next to the cells that need it.

In spinal muscular atrophy type 1, a baby's two SMN1 genes are both faulty, so the nerve cells that drive the muscles waste away, and most of these babies never sit up unaided. Zolgensma, approved in 2019, carries a good SMN1 gene into the body in a single drip into a vein. That only works because of its virus. AAV comes in types whose coat proteins act like address labels, and Zolgensma uses AAV9, the type that can cross from the blood into the brain and spinal cord to reach the motor neurons.

The catch is in the phrase "one shot". The first dose teaches the immune system to recognise that virus's coat, and the antibodies it makes destroy a second dose before it can reach its target. Getting around that is one of the field's biggest open problems.

only-36-of-100.context_blurb:
Science checks itself by repeating experiments. In 2011 psychology put that to the test on a grand scale: about 270 researchers set out to re-run 100 published studies from three leading journals and see which findings held. The answer, published in Science in 2015, shook the field, and the field deserves credit for publishing its own bad news.

The project was led by Brian Nosek, a psychologist at the University of Virginia, who in 2013 had co-founded the Center for Open Science in Charlottesville to make such checks happen. Of the 100 original studies, 97 had reported a real effect. When the re-runs were tallied, only 36 found it again, and even the survivors' effects were about half as large as first reported.

The losses were uneven. Studies of memory and cognition, close to a stopwatch, held up about half the time, while social psychology, the branch full of striking stories about human nature, managed only about a quarter.

Some original authors insisted the effects were genuine but fragile, needing just the right lab or the right students. In 2018 the Many Labs 2 project tested that defence by running 28 classic effects in dozens of countries on some 15,000 people. The pattern was blunt: an effect that replicated did so nearly everywhere, and one that failed, failed nearly everywhere, so hidden local conditions could not explain the misses.

Nor is the problem confined to psychology. In 2016 Monya Baker of Nature surveyed 1,576 scientists, and more than 70 percent said they had at some point been unable to repeat another scientist's experiment. By field, chemists came out worst, with 87 percent reporting such a failure, ahead of biologists at 77 and physicists and engineers at 69. Often the cause is arithmetic, not fraud: small studies chasing small effects cross the line of significance only when luck has already pushed the number too high.

opportunity-and-ingenuity-the-missions-t.context_blurb:
Two small NASA machines on Mars far outlived their plans, and the engineers told honestly why: partly good design, partly luck the designers never modelled. Opportunity, a six-wheeled, solar-powered rover, and Ingenuity, a tiny helicopter, both turned short trial runs into years of exploration.

Opportunity bounced down in January 2004 into Eagle, a little crater on the plain of Meridiani Planum. It was built to last 90 sols, or Martian days, about three months. Its twin, Spirit, had landed three weeks earlier on the far side of the planet; in 2009 Spirit's wheels sank into soft soil at a spot called Troy, and it never drove free.

In Eagle crater Opportunity found the bedrock studded with thousands of little grey balls of haematite, an iron mineral, which looked bluish in false-colour pictures, so the team called them blueberries. Lying beside them were yellow sulfate salts, and on Earth that pair forms in shallow, salty pools, so the verdict was that this ground had once lain under standing acidic water.

The team expected dust to coat the solar panels and starve the rover within months. Instead, passing gusts of Martian wind kept sweeping the panels clean, in what the engineers called cleaning events, and Opportunity worked for more than fourteen years. By the end it had driven about 45 kilometres, a little more than a full marathon, the first one ever run on another world. The same weather finally killed it. In June 2018 a storm of dust lifted from the surface wrapped the whole planet and blacked out the sky for weeks, and Opportunity's final message reached Earth on 10 June.

Ingenuity, a helicopter weighing 1.8 kilograms, faced a harder problem: the Martian air is only about a hundredth as dense as ours at sea level. Lift grows with air density and with the square of blade speed, so its twin 1.2-metre rotors spun at around 2,400 revolutions a minute, roughly ten times as fast as a helicopter's on Earth. Funded for five flights, it flew 72 before a rough landing in 2024 broke its blades. Under its belly it carried a small piece of the cloth that had covered the wings of the Wright brothers' 1903 Flyer.

oxygens-three-discoverers.context_blurb:
Oxygen has three discoverers, and the honest story gives each one a different part. A Swedish apothecary made the gas first, an English minister published it first, and a French chemist understood it first. Their tangle shows how much separates finding something from knowing what you have found.

Joseph Priestley, an English clergyman and chemist, was already famous for his work on gases. In 1771 he let a candle burn out in a sealed jar, put a living sprig of mint inside for several days, and found he could relight a candle in that same air: the plant had restored it. He had glimpsed what we now call photosynthesis.

On 1 August 1774 he focused sunlight through a large lens onto a heap of red mercuric oxide, a compound of mercury, and collected the gas that came off. A candle in it burned dazzlingly bright, and a mouse shut in a jar of it lived far longer than in ordinary air. When he breathed some himself, he wrote that for some time afterwards his breast felt "peculiarly light and easy".

In Sweden the apothecary Carl Wilhelm Scheele had produced that very gas around 1771 or 1772, from other ingredients, and called it fire air. It was oxygen, but his book was stuck with the printer until 1777, by which time the credit had gone elsewhere.

In October 1774 Priestley described his gas over dinner in Paris to his host, Antoine Lavoisier, and repeated the experiment at Lavoisier's bench. Lavoisier ran it again on a precision balance, weighing everything that went in and came out, and concluded that the gas was an element. He named it oxygène and used it to explain burning and breathing.

So historians give each man his own verb: Scheele was the first to make it, Priestley the first to publish it, and Lavoisier the first to understand it. The strangest twist is Priestley's. He never admitted what his gas really was, calling it dephlogisticated air and defending the phlogiston theory, the old idea that burning releases a substance called phlogiston, until his death in 1804. In 1791 a Birmingham mob burned his house and laboratory over his religious and political views, and he ended his life in Pennsylvania.

p-hacking-and-the-garden-of-forking-path.context_blurb:
Most bad science involves no faked numbers at all. It comes from the quiet choices every researcher makes about which data to keep, when to stop and which comparison to report. A run of studies from 2011 onward showed how those honest-looking choices can manufacture almost any result, and what can be done to stop it.

In 2011 three psychologists, Uri Simonsohn, Leif Nelson and Joseph Simmons, proved the point with a deliberately absurd study. In their first experiment, students who heard the Wiggles' children's song "Hot Potato" said they felt older than students who heard a control track. In the second, students who listened to the Beatles' "When I'm Sixty-Four" turned out roughly eighteen months younger, judged by birth date. Nothing was faked. The authors named the source of the trick researcher degrees of freedom: the everyday freedom to choose what to measure, when to stop collecting and what to compare.

They then simulated the damage. Checking the result after every new subject and stopping the moment it crossed the line of significance raised the real false-positive rate from the advertised 5 percent to about 22 percent on its own. Combining four common habits, such as picking the best outcome, adding subjects after a peek, adding a control and dropping a group, pushed it to 60.7 percent. A researcher using all four is more likely than not to find an effect that is not there.

Fiddling after the fact takes other forms. Changing your written prediction after seeing the data, known as HARKing, makes a lucky guess look like a prediction that came true, hiding chance behind a made-up forecast. Andrew Gelman and Eric Loken argued in 2014 that even a sincere researcher who runs only one analysis can be fooled if that analysis was chosen after looking at the data. Their image for it was a garden whose paths keep forking: every fork taken after seeing the data is a choice the reader never sees.

How much do such choices matter? In 2018 a group led by Raphael Silberzahn handed one football dataset to 29 separate teams with a single question: whether dark-skinned players are shown more red cards by referees. Twenty teams found a significant effect and nine did not, with estimates ranging from no effect to nearly triple the odds. Same data, same question, everyone competent, different answers.

These habits are common, not rare crimes. A 2012 survey of over 2,000 psychologists by Leslie John and two colleagues found that more than half had left some of their measures unreported, and the authors' name for such habits was questionable research practices.

The most famous case went further. In 2016 Brian Wansink, a star food scientist at Cornell, boasted online about a student who kept mining one failed pizza-buffet study at his request until it yielded several papers. Statisticians outside his lab took the post as an admission, checked the work, and found it riddled with errors and with data that had been manipulated. Nick Brown, Jordan Anaya and Tim van der Zee counted some 150 numbers in the pizza papers that could not be right. Cornell found misconduct, more than twenty of his papers were retracted or corrected, and he resigned.

Many reforms help, but only one closes the loophole of telling a story after the fact: pre-registration, filing the hypothesis and the analysis plan publicly before any data are collected.

pascal-and-the-weight-of-fluids-the-clai.context_blurb:
In the 1640s a new instrument puzzled Europe: a glass tube of mercury, turned upside down in a dish, whose column stood a little under a metre high with an apparently empty space above it. Blaise Pascal, a young French mathematician, believed the weight of the outside air held the column up, and in 1648 he had the idea tested on a mountain, with a care for method that still looks modern.

His reasoning was simple. If air presses down on the dish, then carrying the tube up a mountain leaves less air overhead, so the mercury must stand shorter on the mountaintop than at its base. He wrote the prediction down in advance and said that any other result would kill his idea. Too ill to climb himself, he sent careful instructions to Florin Périer, his sister's husband and a judge at the tax court of Clermont, who on 19 September 1648 climbed the volcano called the Puy de Dôme. Pascal's letter dealt mostly with method: repeat the reading many times, below and on top, always with one and the same tube and the same mercury, so that only the altitude could change.

Périer had a twin tube set up in the friars' garden below, and Father Chastin kept an eye on it from morning to evening. Through calm, rain, fog and wind, the garden tube never moved from its starting height. That untouched twin was a control: it showed that the weather was not moving the mercury, so whatever happened at the summit came from the mountain. At the top the column stood about 84 millimetres lower. Before trusting the result, Périer tilted and shook the tubes to make sure no hidden air bubble was doing the work, and the reading did not budge. On the way down the mercury climbed back step by step. Pascal printed Périer's letter whole inside his own pamphlet, so that readers could see the raw report rather than his summary of it.

Pascal then checked the rule on a climb anyone in Paris could manage, up Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie's bell tower, some fifty metres high. Between the street and the top, the mercury fell about two lines, roughly four and a half millimetres, just what the mountain's figures predicted for that height. Because pressure falls so faithfully with height, a barometer is also an altitude gauge, and an aircraft's altimeter still works this way. Your ears feel the same physics in a fast lift. As you rise, the gas trapped behind each eardrum pushes outward until the Eustachian tube, a narrow passage linking the middle ear with the back of the throat, opens with a pop and evens out the pressure.

Pascal liked to make people predict before he tested. In Rouen in 1647 he had the glassworks make a water tube and a wine tube, each about forty-five feet tall, and asked the crowd which would stand higher. Followers of Aristotle chose water, reasoning that wine's vapour would press its column down. The wine stood higher, because wine is less dense than water, so a taller column of it is needed to weigh as much as the air's push.

Not everyone accepted that the space above the mercury was empty. The Jesuit Étienne Noël, who had once taught Descartes, argued in 1648 that a fine air seeped into it through invisible pores in the glass, a serious alternative that a good test had to rule out. Descartes himself argued with Pascal in Paris for two days in 1647 and afterwards joked that Pascal had too much vacuum in his head. For Descartes, matter simply is extension, length, breadth and depth, so a stretch of truly empty space would be a contradiction, ruled out by definition before any tube was raised.

Not every Pascal story is true. Textbooks credit him with the barrel-buster, a sealed barrel burst by a few cups of water poured down a tall thin pipe. The physics is real, since pressure depends only on the depth of a liquid, but no trace of it appears in anything Pascal wrote that survives; French schoolbooks attached it to his name in the nineteenth century. His real principle, that pressure pushed into a trapped liquid reaches every part of it at full strength, runs every car jack. Nothing is free, though: the jack pays in distance, so your handle travels perhaps a metre to lift the car a couple of centimetres.

past-the-scissors-base-editing-and-a-the.context_blurb:
Gene editing lets doctors change the DNA inside living cells. The first tools worked like scissors; newer ones work more like a pencil with an eraser, rewriting a single letter. In 2025 one of them saved a baby in Philadelphia, with a medicine designed for him alone.

Classic CRISPR uses an enzyme called Cas9, steered by a short guide RNA, to sever the DNA's double strand completely. The cell's emergency repair then glues the ends back together hastily and sloppily, often adding or losing a few random letters. That is fine for switching a gene off, but useless for fixing one wrong letter. In 2016 David Liu's team at the Broad Institute kept the guide RNA and Cas9's ability to find its address, crippled its cutting, and attached a deaminase, an enzyme that chemically turns one DNA base into another right where it sits. Such base editors can turn a C into a T, or an A into a G.

To write longer stretches, Liu's lab introduced prime editing in 2019. It joins a nicking version of Cas9 to a reverse transcriptase, an enzyme first found in retroviruses, which reads the new sequence carried on an extra-long guide and copies it into the DNA.

In August 2024 a baby boy, KJ Muldoon, was born in Philadelphia with CPS1 deficiency, a rare disorder in which the liver cannot clear ammonia. Rebecca Ahrens-Nicklas and Kiran Musunuru led a team that designed a base editor from scratch for his exact mutation and gave it to him alone, the first therapy of its kind. From diagnosis to first dose took about six months: cell models within one month, the best editor chosen by two, tests in monkeys by five, and a clinical-grade drug cleared by the FDA at six. When the system chooses to move fast, it can.

The team hopes it has built a reusable kit. The base-editor protein, the tiny fat bubble that delivers it and much of the safety work stay the same; only the short guide RNA changes for each new patient's mutation, which could shrink the slow work of finding targets and manufacturing every time. How regulators will treat each new version is still an open question.

pasteurs-swan-neck-flask.context_blurb:
For two thousand years people believed that simple life could spring from dead matter on its own: maggots from meat, mould from bread, microbes from broth. The idea was called spontaneous generation. In the 1860s Louis Pasteur all but killed it with a glass flask whose neck curved like a swan's, an experiment a kitchen can copy.

The doubts began with Francesco Redi in 1668. He set out jars of meat, some uncovered and some under a layer of fine gauze. Flies, drawn by the smell, laid their eggs on the gauze, and the maggots hatched there, never in the meat beneath. But microscopes soon showed life swarming in sealed liquids no fly could reach. In 1765 Lazzaro Spallanzani sealed broth and boiled it for up to an hour, and nothing grew. John Needham, whose briefly boiled flasks had teemed with life, replied that the long boil had destroyed a vital force in the trapped air, a claim no one could test.

By 1860 the quarrel had two champions in France, Pasteur and Félix Pouchet, and the Academy of Sciences forced the issue by offering a cash prize for a decisive experiment. Pouchet, director of the natural history museum at Rouen, was no crank. He claimed a litre of air taken anywhere would breed life in broth, and he gathered air on the plains of Sicily, on Mount Etna and out at sea to prove it.

Pasteur's answer was the swan-neck flask. He boiled broth in flasks left open to the air, but drew each neck out into a long, drooping S-bend. Air could drift in, yet its dust dropped out in the curve of the neck, and the broth stayed clear for months. When he tipped one so the broth sloshed up into the curve and returned, it swarmed with life within a day, because it had picked up the dust lodged in the bend.

He also carried sealed, sterile flasks up mountains and opened them. Eight of twenty spoiled on a valley road near Arbois and five of twenty at 850 metres. Up on the glacier called the Mer de Glace, some 2,000 metres high, only one of twenty spoiled, and he reported that single failure instead of hiding it. The first attempt on the glacier failed: the glare off the snow made the flame of his spirit lamp invisible, so he could not melt the flasks shut.

Pouchet hit back in the Pyrenees. After opening his first phials at 2,083 metres, just above Pasteur's height, his party slept out in bitter cold and climbed at dawn to a glacier at 3,000 metres, where every phial he opened grew life. He was honest; the difference was in the flasks. Pouchet used hay water, and hay harbours hardy spores that come through a boiling alive, a fact nobody understood until the 1870s.

Pasteur was careful about what his flasks showed. In his 1860 report he only hoped that the work might prepare the road for serious research into the causes of disease; he linked microbes to contagion years later.

pasteurs-tweezers-the-day-molecules-grew.context_blurb:
In 1848 a 25-year-old chemist in Paris, Louis Pasteur, showed that a molecule can exist in two mirror-image versions, one left-handed and one right-handed, which cannot be laid one on top of the other, like your two hands. He did it with a heap of crystals, a magnifying lens and a pair of tweezers, and the puzzle he opened is still unsolved.

The puzzle had a name: paratartaric acid. In 1844 Eilhard Mitscherlich reported that it matched ordinary tartaric acid, from wine casks, in every way, except that tartaric acid twists a beam of polarized light and paratartaric did not. Pasteur had already examined nineteen other compounds, and in every one the tiny extra facets on the crystals all leaned the same way. So when the paratartrate salt showed facets leaning both ways, he treated the split heap as a discovery, not dirt.

He sorted the crystals by hand, one at a time, with tweezers and a lens, into a left-leaning pile and a right-leaning pile. Dissolved separately, one pile twisted light to the right and the other to the left; mixed back together they cancelled out. Paratartaric acid was simply equal amounts of two mirror-image forms whose opposite turns cancel. His son-in-law's biography says he then grabbed a museum curator he met in a corridor and hauled him out into the Luxembourg Gardens to explain, a scene only that family book records.

The great physicist Jean-Baptiste Biot, then 74, would not take it on trust. He had Pasteur repeat everything in his own laboratory, insisting that the acid, soda and ammonia all come from his own stock. He made Pasteur state in advance which pile would turn light which way. When Biot saw the left-turning solution in his instrument, he gripped Pasteur's arm and said, as Pasteur told it, that he had loved science so much all his life that this made his heart throb.

Pasteur also had luck, and knew it. The crystals had to be grown in the morning, because the day's warmth partly redissolved them and wiped out the tiny facets. Above about 28 °C this salt does not form separate left and right crystals at all; instead, left and right forms build one shared crystal together. At Lille in 1854 he said that in observation, chance favours only the prepared mind.

Because each dissolved pile kept its twist even after the crystal shapes were gone, Pasteur concluded that handedness must belong to the shape of each molecule, decades before anyone could draw a molecule's shape. Life, he found, can tell the hands apart. In 1860 he fed a 50-50 mix of the two tartrate forms to the mould Penicillium glaucum, and the mould consumed the right-handed form, leaving the left-handed form behind.

Life is one-handed throughout: nearly all the amino acids in proteins are left-handed, and the sugars in DNA and RNA right-handed, while ordinary chemistry makes both in equal amounts. Why life chose one hand, the honest answer is that nobody knows yet: several ideas are still in play and none has won out.

paulis-ghost-the-particle-invented-to-sa.context_blurb:
In 1930 physics had a leak. In beta decay a nucleus throws out an electron, and some energy seemed to vanish. Wolfgang Pauli proposed that an unseen particle was carrying it off. That particle, the neutrino, took twenty-six years to catch and is still not fully understood.

The leak had shown up in 1914. Every alpha particle a given atom emits leaves with one fixed energy. But when Chadwick measured beta-decay electrons, their energies formed a continuous smear, from almost nothing up to a sharp top limit. Only the fastest electrons accounted for all the energy. Niels Bohr was ready to give ground on the law itself: perhaps energy is conserved on average, not in every single decay.

Pauli preferred a particle. On 4 December 1930 he wrote an open letter to a meeting of radioactivity experts in Tübingen, proposing a tiny neutral particle that slipped away with the missing energy. He did not attend, explaining that he was needed in Zurich for a ball. He called his idea a desperate remedy and did not dare publish it. He named the particle a neutron, but in 1932 Chadwick found a heavy neutral particle in the atomic nucleus and the word went to that, so Enrico Fermi's circle in Rome renamed Pauli's ghost the neutrino, the little neutral one.

Neutrinos barely touch anything. Tens of billions from the Sun pass through each square centimetre of you every second, yet over a whole lifetime only one or two will interact with your body. In 1936 Hans Bethe and Robert Bacher judged them practically undetectable, but named one reaction a neutrino can certainly cause: hitting a proton and changing it into a neutron, inverse beta decay.

Frederick Reines and Clyde Cowan set out to catch one. Their first plan, approved in 1951, used a 20-kiloton bomb test: the detector would hang in a deep vacuum tank and, at the moment of the blast, be cut loose to fall freely so the ground shock passed it by. They switched to a nuclear reactor instead. At Hanford in 1953, when a team member widened a test well in the detector to fit a person, everyone they lowered in set the counters ticking, thanks to the radioactive potassium-40 present naturally in every human body. The Hanford run failed for a different reason: cosmic rays pouring through the roof swamped the signal whether the reactor was on or off.

At Savannah River in 1956 they buried the detector deep and demanded a signature no stray particle could fake. A neutrino striking a proton makes a positron, which flashes at once, and a neutron, which wanders a few microseconds before being captured with a second, brighter flash. Only two flashes, microseconds apart and in that order, counted. It worked, and they cabled the news to Pauli.

Even then the story was unfinished. For about thirty years Ray Davis counted solar neutrinos in a vast tank of cleaning fluid deep in a South Dakota gold mine and found only about a third of what the Sun should be sending, according to John Bahcall's calculations. The Sun was fine; the neutrinos were changing into other kinds of neutrino on the way to Earth. One question remains open. Deep underground, detectors watch for a kind of double beta decay that would release no neutrinos at all. A single such decay would prove the neutrino is its own antiparticle, and none has yet been seen.

pcr-the-idea-on-highway-128.context_blurb:
PCR, short for polymerase chain reaction, can copy one stretch of DNA into billions, and it now runs in every crime lab, hospital and genetics lab on Earth. The idea came to the American biochemist Kary Mullis on a night drive in 1983. Making it work took a bacterium from a hot spring, and using it safely took lessons nobody expected.

Heading for his cabin in Mendocino County one Friday night in 1983, Mullis was on Highway 128 when the scheme came to him. He stopped at mile marker 46.7 and worked it out on paper and a pen from the glove compartment. At a second stop he saw that the primers could be aimed at whatever stretch of DNA he liked. Jennifer Barnett, his girlfriend and a trained chemist, slept in the passenger seat through the whole thing; he tried to wake her, and she would not wake up. At the cabin, too excited to sleep, he drew diagrams on every flat surface that would take pen, pencil or crayon until dawn.

The power is in the doubling. Heat splits DNA's two strands; on cooling, two short synthetic primers latch onto either end of the target; a polymerase enzyme fills in the rest; and every cycle doubles the copies. Ten cycles make a thousand, twenty a million, thirty a billion, and Mullis noticed that a billion is close to the number of base pairs in the human genome. In practice the climb stalls after some 25 to 30 rounds, because the primers and the loose DNA building blocks get used up.

It looked too easy, so he spent the weekend hunting for the flaw. On Monday he searched the library for any earlier paper on copying DNA this way and found nothing at all, neither success nor failure. His first real test, begun around midnight in early September 1983, used human DNA and a single round of heating, and the gel next day showed no band at the expected 400 base pairs. The heating and cooling had to be repeated again and again. Worse, the heat that split the strands also destroyed the enzyme, so for years a technician had to add fresh enzyme by hand at every cycle.

The rescue came from pure curiosity. In the 1960s Thomas Brock went to Yellowstone asking how hot water could be and still hold living things, and in 1967 he concluded that there was no way to set an upper temperature limit for life. In 1966 Brock and a student of his, Hudson Freeze, had taken a bacterium, Thermus aquaticus, from Mushroom Spring, a hot spring in Yellowstone. In 1985 Cetus scientists purified its heat-proof polymerase, Taq, and a sealed tube could at last be cycled and left alone.

Recognition came slowly. Science rejected Mullis's own paper describing the method outright; three years later the same journal named PCR its Molecule of the Year. Cetus, which owned the patents, gave Mullis a bonus of $10,000, and in 1991 Hoffmann-La Roche paid it $300 million for PCR. Mullis won a share of the chemistry Nobel in 1993.

PCR copies a stray molecule as faithfully as the one you want. Across Germany, Austria and France, detectives spent sixteen years chasing the "Phantom of Heilbronn", a woman whose DNA appeared at over forty crime scenes, among them a policewoman's murder. In 2009 the trail collapsed: the DNA belonged to a worker on the production line of the company making the police's cotton swabs, which were sterile but not free of human DNA. Hospital PCR labs therefore split work across separate rooms with traffic in one direction only, chiefly to keep out the most dangerous contaminant of all, leftover product from an earlier run, which holds billions of copies of exactly the sequence being sought.

Mullis later denied that HIV causes AIDS, complaining that no single paper proved it. A count answers him. In the Multicenter AIDS Cohort Study, researchers measured the immune cells whose loss marks AIDS more than 22,000 times in men without HIV, and saw those cells collapse in just one case. A Nobel Prize rewards one piece of work; it does not make its winner right about everything else.

peer-review-is-a-smell-test-not-a-truth-.context_blurb:
Peer review, in which outside experts judge a paper before it is printed, is often treated as a seal of truth. Its record says something humbler. It improves papers, but it has waved through famous frauds, and those frauds were caught by readers outside the system who checked the evidence for themselves.

The system is younger than most people think. Newton, Darwin and Einstein published without it, and Nature did not insist on outside referees until 1973; before that, the editor decided alone. When Einstein and Nathan Rosen submitted a paper to Physical Review in 1936, the editor, John Tate, took the then-unusual step of passing it to an anonymous referee. Einstein withdrew it in fury, complaining that Tate had shown his manuscript to specialists before publication. The referee, Howard Percy Robertson, had in fact caught a real error, and Einstein quietly fixed it.

Piltdown shows how a fake can fit expectations. In 1912 the amateur Charles Dawson and the British Museum geologist Arthur Smith Woodward unveiled a skull dug from a gravel pit in Sussex as the long-sought link between apes and humans. It suited the leading theory, which expected a big, human-looking brain to have evolved ahead of an ape-like jaw and body. In 1953 Kenneth Oakley measured the fluorine the bones had soaked up from the soil and found wildly different levels in the skull and the jaw, so they could not be from one creature. Wilfrid Le Gros Clark and Joseph Weiner then found, under a microscope, file marks where the teeth had been ground down. In 2016 Isabelle De Groote's team used DNA to show that every planted tooth came from one single orangutan, the mark of a single forger, most likely Dawson.

Peer review has been tested directly. When editors plant deliberate errors in a paper and send it out, reviewers catch only about one in three on average. The journalist John Bohannon, in 2013, sent a made-up study of a lichen-based cancer drug, riddled with obvious flaws, to 304 open-access journals, and 157 accepted it.

The great frauds were caught by readers. At Bell Labs around 2001, Jan Hendrik Schön turned out a new paper about once a week, many in Nature and Science, until other physicists noticed the very same noise curve appearing in different experiments. At Tilburg University the social psychologist Diederik Stapel invented data for years, until three young researchers from his own department reported him. In 2020 The Lancet printed a study of some 96,000 COVID-19 patients supplied by the company Surgisphere; outside readers found that Surgisphere had only about eleven employees and that its Australian figures were impossible, and the paper was retracted within three weeks.

So what is peer review good for? Controlled studies find that at its best it reliably improves how a paper reports its methods and how clearly it is written. It is a smell test by two or three busy strangers who never see the raw data: useful, but not a truth detector.

perkins-purple-accident.context_blurb:
In 1856 William Henry Perkin, a London student of eighteen, tried to make a malaria drug and made the world's first synthetic dye instead. His purple, made from the tar left over by gasworks, launched the chemical dye industry and, through it, much of modern medicine, along with some of the first industrial diseases.

London lit its streets with coal gas from 1813, and the gasworks left mountains of black tar that nobody wanted, so the works simply poured it, with their other liquid waste, into the Thames. Chemists began to mine it. In 1834 Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge distilled from coal tar a clear oily liquid, later named aniline, and when he added bleaching powder it turned a vivid blue in a flash.

Malaria was common even in London: at St Thomas's Hospital in 1853 it accounted for about a quarter of admissions. The one reliable treatment, quinine, came from the bark of cinchona, a South American tree, and it was scarce and costly. In 1849 August Wilhelm von Hofmann, who ran the Royal College of Chemistry in London, suggested building quinine from cheap aniline, and he later set his young assistant Perkin on the problem. The plan rested on counting atoms: if the chemical formulas balanced, Perkin assumed, the right molecule should follow. But the same atoms can be arranged into quite different molecules, and in 1856 nobody yet knew how molecules were shaped.

Over Easter 1856, in a small laboratory at the top of his family's house, Perkin's attempt gave only a black sludge. Instead of throwing it away he added alcohol, and it gave a brilliant purple solution. Silk dyed with it kept its colour through washing and sunlight. Chemistry later explained his luck: his aniline, distilled from coal tar, was contaminated with toluidines, and their extra methyl groups are built into the dye molecule itself, so pure aniline would never have given mauve.

He sent dyed silk to Pullar's, a Perth dyeing firm, and Robert Pullar called it one of the most valuable discoveries in a long while, on one condition: that it did not make the goods too expensive. Perkin patented it at eighteen. Hofmann urged him not to leave academic chemistry for trade, but Perkin talked his father, a carpenter and builder, into staking the family's savings on a factory, which was running by the end of 1857. Purple, once the costliest colour on Earth, became a craze; by 1859 the magazine Punch was mocking it as the mauve measles.

Perkin never knew exactly what he had made. Only in 1994 did chemists show that mauveine is not one compound but a mixture of a dozen or more closely related salts. The dye industry also gave medicine a start. In 1932, at the German combine IG Farben, Gerhard Domagk tested compounds on infected mice and found that a red textile dye cured them; sold as Prontosil, it was the first drug to cure a bacterial infection. The same chemistry had a cost. In 1895 the Frankfurt surgeon Ludwig Rehn reported bladder cancer in three of 45 workers from the room where Hoechst made magenta, and a surgeon employed by the company stood up and contradicted him at the same meeting. Rehn was right: dye work became one of the first known occupational cancers.

perpetual-motion-always-fails.context_blurb:
A perpetual motion machine would run forever, or give out more energy than it takes in. People have claimed to build them for at least eight hundred years, and every one has failed or turned out to be a trick. The useful question about any such machine is always the same: what is secretly going in?

In 1812 and 1813 Charles Redheffer showed a self-turning machine for money in Philadelphia. When eight city inspectors came to judge it, he let them look only through a barred window. The inspector's son, Coleman Sellers, noticed which face of the cog teeth was worn: the face that wears only on a gear doing the driving, so the gear Redheffer called the output was actually pushing the machine. To make the point in public, Nathan Sellers had the engineer Isaiah Lukens build a fake perpetual machine secretly driven by clockwork, and when Redheffer saw it he offered to buy it on the spot.

Redheffer moved to New York. There the steamboat builder Robert Fulton watched the machine and, without touching it, called it a fraud: its turning was jerky and uneven, as if a person were driving it, where a true machine runs smoothly. He pulled boards from the wall beside it and followed a catgut cord to the floor above, where, as the story is always told, an old man sat turning a hand crank with one hand and eating a crust of bread with the other.

Some devices only look perpetual, and the test is to find the input. A drinking bird bobs for hours on the evaporation of water from its felt head; trap it under a jar until the air inside is saturated, and it stops. Arthur Beverly's clock at the University of Otago has run unwound since 1864, powered by a sealed box of air that swells and shrinks as the room's temperature rises and falls.

The oldest fraud-free failure is the overbalanced wheel. Bhaskara II, a mathematician of twelfth-century India, sketched one with curved spokes holding mercury that would slide outward on the falling side. It never works, because the side whose weights reach farther out always carries fewer of them, and reach times weight comes out even on both sides. Johann Bessler's great wheel at Weissenstein Castle ran for weeks in a locked, sealed room in 1717 and 1718, and he asked a fortune for the secret. In 1727 his maid testified under oath that she had turned it by hand from the next room, in shifts with Bessler's family.

Physics rules out even cleverer schemes. A ship drawing heat from the ocean to drive itself can never work, because any heat engine has to dump part of its heat into something colder. John Keely of Philadelphia raised millions for a motor he said freed an "etheric force" from drops of water. When his gun fired a lead ball through planking in 1884, the ordnance officer Edmund Zalinski said ordinary compressed air could have done the very same. After Keely died in 1898, engineers and physicists hired by a newspaper took his workshop apart and found hidden tubing and valves beneath the floor, which he had worked with his foot.

The claims continue. In 2006 the Irish company Steorn challenged scientists to test its free-energy device, Orbo, and 420 volunteered within a day and a half. At its public demonstration in London in July 2007 nothing turned, and the company put the failure down to heat from the stage lights. When Joseph Newman sued after the Patent Office rejected his Energy Machine, a court had the National Bureau of Standards test it in 1986: in every test, the power coming out was less than the batteries put in. The U.S. Patent Office keeps a standing bet. Its examiners' manual asks perpetual-motion inventors, and only them, for a model that actually runs, demonstrated before the examiner, and nobody has ever collected.
