phineas-gage-the-rod-and-the-story-that-.context_blurb:
In September 1848 an explosion on a railway job in Vermont drove an iron bar more than a metre long through the head of Phineas Gage, the foreman, and he lived. He became the most famous patient in brain science, the man whose personality supposedly changed. The documents tell a more careful, and more hopeful, story than the legend.

The 13-pound tamping iron entered under his left cheekbone and came out through the top of his skull. Gage was talking within minutes. His men lifted him into an ox cart, and he rode to his hotel sitting up. When the first doctor, Edward Williams, arrived, Gage reportedly greeted him by saying there was business enough here for him, a line known only from Williams's later memory. An hour after reaching the hotel, Gage climbed a long staircase to his bed on his own feet. That night Dr John Harlow pushed a finger down into the wound from the top of the head and another up through the hole in the cheek, and the two fingers nearly met.

Gage survived infection and was up and about by the start of 1849. He had lost the sight of his left eye, and on top of his head Harlow recorded a dent through which the brain could be seen pulsing. City surgeons thought the case a physiological impossibility; before they would believe the country doctor, they demanded signed statements vouching for it from clergymen and lawyers. Then the Harvard surgeon Henry Bigelow brought Gage to Boston, examined him for weeks and published the case. Gage gave his iron to Harvard's medical museum engraved with an inscription that misspells his name, misdates the accident by a day and claims he had fully recovered from the injury.

For a while Gage showed himself and his iron for money, at Barnum's American Museum in New York, not at Barnum's circus, which did not yet exist. His mother later said that his strongest attachment of all was to the tamping iron, which stayed his constant companion for the rest of his life. Then he went to Chile, where for years he drove a six-horse coach between Valparaíso and Santiago: thirteen hours a day, horses harnessed before dawn, luggage loaded, and every passenger's fare collected and change given. A doctor there described him as healthy, with no impairment of his mind.

The famous portrait of a rude, unreliable Gage, no longer himself, comes from a paper Harlow read in 1868. By then Gage had died in California eight years earlier, and the paper described observations made two decades before. A 2022 review of 25 modern scientific papers found that 24 blamed his change entirely on brain damage; only one raised the possibility that his disfigurement and the way people shunned him had changed him.

Even the damage is argued over, because no autopsy was ever done. In 1994 Hanna Damasio's team modelled the wound on a different skull and said both frontal lobes were hit. A 2004 CT study of the real skull by Ion-Florin Talos and Peter Ratiu found damage to the left frontal lobe only, with the ventricles and major blood vessels spared. The only known photograph of Gage surfaced in 2008, when the collectors Jack and Beverly Wilgus, who had thought it showed a whaler with a harpoon, matched the writing on the pole he holds to the inscription on Harvard's tamping iron.

photo-51-and-the-honest-credit-story.context_blurb:
Photo 51 is an X-ray picture of DNA taken in London in 1952, and it helped reveal that the molecule of life is a double helix. It was made by Rosalind Franklin, a chemist at King's College London, and her student Raymond Gosling. How it reached the men who won the Nobel Prize is a story worth telling exactly.

Franklin first made her name on coal. From 1942 she measured the tiny pores inside it by pushing gases in, and found that heating coal tightens the pores' narrow necks until, above about 1,000 °C, even helium, the smallest atom of all, is locked out.

At King's she used DNA from a very pure batch prepared by Rudolf Signer, a Swiss chemist, from calf thymus, a gland in a young cow's chest, which could be drawn into fine, even fibres. DNA has a dry A form and a wet B form, the shape it takes in living cells, which holds only in very humid air. Franklin built a sealed chamber and set its humidity by passing bubbles of hydrogen through salt solutions, so the fibres kept their wet shape for days on end. Gosling operated the camera to her protocols, and the exposure for the famous picture lasted about sixty-two hours. The name is just a filing number: it was picture number fifty-one in Franklin's numbered series of DNA images.

The film showed an X of dark spots stretching from corner to corner, a pattern that only a helix produces. The spacing of the spots gave the size of the turns, and their brightness put the heavy sugar-phosphate chains on the molecule's outer surface and the bases facing in. Even an absence spoke: on each arm of the cross the fourth spot is missing, which means the two strands are staggered along the axis by roughly three-eighths of a turn.

Meanwhile in Cambridge, James Watson and Francis Crick were building models. In November 1951 Watson heard Franklin present her results and took no notes; the three-chain model he and Crick then built had the water content badly wrong, and Franklin took it apart. Their director, Lawrence Bragg, ordered the pair off DNA entirely. By January 1953 Franklin was leaving King's and had handed the work to Maurice Wilkins. On 30 January Wilkins showed Watson Photo 51 without telling Franklin. A research council report carrying her measurements also reached Crick through Max Perutz. In it Crick spotted the crystal symmetry called face-centred monoclinic, which he knew from horse haemoglobin, and saw that DNA's two chains must run in opposite directions.

Franklin's own paper ran third of three in Nature in April 1953. She moved to Birkbeck College, where her X-ray pictures of tobacco mosaic virus, the best yet made of any virus, showed that its RNA lies embedded in the protein coat, some distance out from the rod's hollow axis. Ovarian cancer killed her in 1958, at 37. Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize, and she could not be included, because the Nobel is never awarded to someone who has died. Watson's 1968 memoir mocked her as "Rosy", but in an epilogue to the same book he conceded that his portrait of her had been unjust.

piltdown-man-forty-years-of-a-fake-ances.context_blurb:
For forty years Britain's most celebrated fossil was a fake. Piltdown Man, taken from a gravel pit in Sussex and presented in 1912, was celebrated as a creature halfway between apes and ourselves. How it fooled the experts, and how chemistry and the microscope finally exposed it, is a lesson in how science corrects itself, slowly.

Charles Dawson, a solicitor and amateur collector, brought the bones to Arthur Smith Woodward of the British Museum, and they unveiled them to London's geologists in 1912. Woodward later wrote a book calling the creature the earliest Englishman. Part of its appeal was pride: Germany had the Neanderthals and France had Cro-Magnon. It also fitted the leading theory, which held that a modern-sized brain had evolved first, long before the jaw and the rest of the body caught up.

Doubters spoke early. In 1913 the Edinburgh anatomist David Waterston wrote in Nature that skull and jaw could not come from one creature, and later the German anatomist Franz Weidenreich called the jaw an orangutan's. The worst cost came in 1925, when Raymond Dart described the Taung Child from South Africa, small-brained but upright, the opposite of Piltdown. Britain's experts mostly dismissed it as a young ape and went on teaching the Sussex skull, and the search for human origins stayed fixed on Europe for another twenty years.

Chemistry ended it. In 1949 Kenneth Oakley tested the bones for fluorine, which buried bones soak up from groundwater over time. It gives relative dating: it shows whether bones from the same site have lain there equally long, not their age in years. The bones proved far younger than claimed, and sharper tests showed that skull and jaw did not match. In 1953 Oakley, Joseph Weiner and Wilfrid Le Gros Clark added a nitrogen test, which measures the protein left in a bone, and the jaw still held about as much as a modern bone. Under a microscope the molars showed criss-crossing scratches that no jaw movement could have produced: someone had filed them flat and stained the pieces to match the gravel. Piltdown was a human braincase only a few centuries old, joined to the jaw of an orangutan.

Who did it? In 2016 Isabelle De Groote's team used DNA to show that a canine from the original pit and a molar from another site nearby were from one and the same orangutan, an animal from southwest Sarawak on Borneo, pointing to a single forger. Dawson was present at every find, and when he died in August 1916, the finds stopped for good. Hoaxes are caught faster now. In 1999 National Geographic unveiled Archaeoraptor, a supposed link between dinosaurs and birds, and within months CT scans revealed it had been assembled from pieces of different fossils.

plancks-act-of-despair.context_blurb:
Every hot object glows, and the colour of that glow is set by its temperature alone. Explaining the exact shape of that glow defeated nineteenth-century physics until, in 1900, the German physicist Max Planck took a step he hated: he assumed energy comes in tiny packets. That step began quantum theory.

You can see the rule on a winter night in Orion. Betelgeuse, on Orion's shoulder, glows orange-red at about 3,800 kelvin; Rigel, on his foot, burns over three times hotter and shines blue-white. Hotter means bluer, so a star's colour is a thermometer. To study the glow cleanly, Gustav Kirchhoff in 1859 imagined a perfect absorber, a blackbody, built as a closed, opaque box with a single small hole: light entering the hole bounces around inside and almost never gets out. He proved from thermodynamics alone that holes in such cavities, at one temperature, glow exactly alike whether the walls are iron, clay or charcoal, though the bare surfaces of those materials do not. One universal curve, then, for every glowing thing.

Two rules came first. In 1893 Wilhelm Wien showed that the wavelength where the glow is brightest falls to half whenever the temperature doubles, which is why a heated poker goes from red toward white. Josef Stefan in 1879, with Ludwig Boltzmann's proof in 1884, found that total output rises with the fourth power of temperature, so doubling a star's temperature makes it pour out sixteen times as much energy.

Classical physics failed at the full curve. Applied by Lord Rayleigh and James Jeans, it gave every vibration in the cavity the same average share of energy, and since a cavity holds endless short-wave vibrations, it predicted endless energy at short wavelengths. Paul Ehrenfest later called this the ultraviolet catastrophe, but it was not what drove Planck. The pressure came from the long-wave end. Heinrich Rubens had learned to isolate far-infrared light by bouncing a beam off several crystals in a row, since each reflection kept mostly the wavelengths the crystal reflects best. With Ferdinand Kurlbaum he found that at those long wavelengths the energy simply rose in a straight line with temperature, which the accepted formula did not allow. On Sunday 7 October 1900 Rubens told Planck about it over dinner, and before the night was over Planck had found a new formula and posted it to Rubens on a card. It fitted all the data.

To make the formula work, Planck had to assume that matter trades energy with light only in whole packets, whose size is set by a brand-new natural constant. He fitted that constant to laboratory oven data, and his figure came within about one percent of the exact value fixed in 2019. He did not like his own move. In a 1931 letter to Robert Williams Wood he called it an act of desperation. For years after 1900 he tried, in what he called unavailing attempts, to squeeze the packets back into the old physics, and only around 1908 did he give up. The curve itself had the last word. In 1990 the COBE satellite measured the dim microwave glow that fills the whole sky, the leftover heat of the Big Bang, and found it fitted Planck's curve more tightly than the thickness of the drawn line.

plasma-the-fourth-state-and-the-one-nobo.context_blurb:
School posters show three states of matter: solid, liquid and gas. Yet lightning, the glow of a neon sign and the Sun itself are none of these. They are plasma, the fourth state of matter, and by far the commonest form of ordinary matter in the universe.

A plasma forms when heat or electricity tears atoms apart into free electrons and positive ions. Those free charges let it carry an electric current, and because every particle is charged, a magnet can bend it, which an ordinary gas cannot do.

The idea is older than the word. In Sheffield in August 1879 the British chemist William Crookes showed glass tubes, almost empty of air, that glowed when high voltage ran through them, and argued that the glowing stuff was a fourth state of matter; he called it radiant matter, and today we call it plasma. He was wrong about the details, since the glow came from electrons rather than charged molecules, but right about the big idea.

The name came in 1928 from Irving Langmuir at General Electric. A colleague recalled that Langmuir chose it because the ionised gas carried its electrons the way blood plasma, the pale fluid of the blood, carries red and white blood cells.

Posters often say that 99 percent of the universe is plasma. That needs a qualifier, because the dark matter and dark energy that make up most of the cosmos are not plasma. The true claim is narrower: of ordinary matter, the stuff of stars and gas clouds, over 99 percent is plasma.

plutos-demotion.context_blurb:
Pluto was found in 1930 and counted as the ninth planet for 76 years, until astronomers voted in 2006 to call it something else. Its story shows how classification follows discovery: the more we find, the more our categories have to change.

Clyde Tombaugh, a young Kansas farm boy hired by Lowell Observatory in Arizona, photographed the same patch of sky on different nights and flicked between the plates looking for a dot that moved. On 18 February 1930 he found one, the world now called Pluto. The name came from an 11-year-old Oxford girl, Venetia Burney, who suggested Pluto over breakfast; her grandfather passed it on, and it won a unanimous vote.

Tombaugh had been hunting Percival Lowell's Planet X, whose pull was supposed to explain how Uranus strayed from its predicted path, and Pluto turned up close to one of Lowell's positions. But Pluto is about a five-hundredth of Earth's mass, far too small to tug on Uranus at all, so the match was luck. The wobbles themselves vanished in 1989, when Voyager 2 showed that Neptune is about half a percent less massive than astronomers had assumed; with the right mass, Uranus's orbit needed no Planet X.

It had happened before. In 1801 Giuseppe Piazzi found Ceres between Mars and Jupiter, and it was called a planet for decades, until dozens of similar bodies turned up nearby and astronomers grouped them all as asteroids. In 2005 Mike Brown's team found Eris beyond Pluto; it proved a hair smaller across, yet roughly 27 percent heavier. That forced the question. At a meeting in Prague in 2006, the International Astronomical Union defined a planet as a body that orbits the Sun, is round under its own gravity, and has cleared its orbital neighbourhood of other bodies, and Pluto, sharing its region with thousands of icy worlds, fails that third test. Alan Stern and other planetary scientists still argue for a definition that would restore it.

Pluto is no dead ice ball. When New Horizons flew past on 14 July 2015 it found ice mountains and a vast heart-shaped plain of nitrogen ice, Sputnik Planitia, with almost no craters. Since craters pile up over time, something must be resurfacing the plain right now, probably slow churning in the solid nitrogen, and what powers it on so small and cold a world, no one yet knows.

polarization-the-hidden-direction-in-lig.context_blurb:
Light is a wave that wobbles from side to side as it travels, and the direction of that wobble, its polarisation, is invisible to human eyes. Yet bees navigate by it, sunglasses and screens depend on it, and engineers once used it to see the stress inside a bridge.

In 1808 the French army engineer Étienne-Louis Malus looked at the sunset reflected in the windows of the Luxembourg Palace through a crystal of Iceland spar. The crystal normally shows everything twice, but as he turned it, one Sun of the pair dimmed and vanished: reflection had lined up the light's wobble, and Malus named the effect polarisation. Iceland spar doubles things because it splits incoming light into two rays, one for each direction of wobble, which bend by different amounts and travel through the crystal at different angles.

Polarising filters were once heavy crystal prisms. In 1929 a Harvard student, Edwin Land, fixed millions of microscopic crystals, all pointing the same way, in a sheet of plastic, and he went on to found the Polaroid company, later famous for instant photographs. Every LCD screen uses polarising filters: each pixel holds a twistable liquid crystal between two crossed polarising filters, and a voltage decides whether the crystal turns the light's wobble enough to pass the second filter. Tilt polarised sunglasses in front of a laptop and at one angle the screen goes black.

Your own eye can catch polarisation. Stare at a plain white area of an LCD screen, or at blue sky ninety degrees from the Sun, and you may notice a faint yellow bowtie: Haidinger's brush, named for the Austrian mineralogist who reported it in 1844. Bees do far better. Karl von Frisch showed in 1949 that a honeybee under cloud reads the direction in which the sky's scattered daylight is wobbling, work that helped win him a Nobel Prize in 1973.

Engineers used it too. From David Brewster's discovery in 1816 until the 1930s, they cut models of bridges and dams from clear plastic and set them between two polarising filters. Squeezed, the plastic blazed with coloured fringes that mapped where the load put it under the greatest internal stress.

The Viking sunstone remains a claim without proof. Sagas mention a sunstone for finding the Sun in fog, and calcite could really do the job, yet two centuries of Norse archaeology have turned up not a single specimen. The only such crystal found beside navigation gear came from an English warship wrecked in 1592.

pouilly-le-fort-the-test-he-announced-in.context_blurb:
In May 1881, on a farm called Pouilly-le-Fort near Melun in France, Louis Pasteur staked his reputation on a public test of his anthrax vaccine, announcing the outcome in advance. A sceptical veterinarian, Hippolyte Rossignol, had proposed the trial expecting to humiliate him.

The principle behind the vaccine came from an accident in 1879. A batch of chicken-cholera germs sat forgotten in the lab over a summer holiday, open to the air. Injected into chickens afterwards, the stale culture left the birds healthy, and they later survived a fresh, deadly dose: the weakened germ had made them immune.

At Pouilly-le-Fort, Pasteur vaccinated half the sheep in May and left the rest as controls, then gave every animal a lethal dose of live anthrax. On 2 June the crowd found the unvaccinated sheep dead and the vaccinated ones grazing.

A century later the historian Gerald Geison read Pasteur's notebooks. The trial was genuine, but the vaccine had not been made by Pasteur's announced oxygen method: his assistant Charles Chamberland had weakened the anthrax with potassium dichromate, a technique taken from Toussaint, a rival.

prophecies-with-dates-on-them.context_blurb:
A forecast with a date on it can be checked by anyone with a calendar, including the person who made it. That is what makes it science. Over the last sixty years famous predictions about famine, resources, sea ice and rising seas have come due, and grading them honestly cuts in more than one direction.

The physicist Richard Feynman gave the rule in his 1974 Caltech commencement talk: the first principle of science is not to fool yourself, since you are the easiest person of all to fool. A dated forecast makes that principle checkable.

In 1968 the Stanford biologist Paul Ehrlich published The Population Bomb, which opened by declaring that in the 1970s hundreds of millions would die of starvation, whatever crash programmes were started. He doubted India could ever feed itself. But in 1965 Norman Borlaug had already shipped hundreds of tons of short-stemmed wheat seed from his program in Mexico to India and Pakistan; short, stiff stems could carry heavy heads of grain without falling over. India's wheat crop roughly quadrupled in twenty years. Borlaug had sped up his breeding in Mexico by running two sites, a warm lowland valley and a high plateau, doubling his breeding seasons to two crops of wheat each year.

In 1980 the economist Julian Simon challenged Ehrlich to a bet. Ehrlich picked five metals; if their prices after inflation rose over ten years, Simon would pay, and if they fell, Ehrlich would. All five fell, and in October 1990 Simon received a cheque for $576.07, with no letter. One decade is one sample, though. Economists later checked 98 ten-year windows between 1910 and 2007 and found Ehrlich would have won most of them, about 61 percent, though measuring prices in hours of work flips the result back toward Simon.

In December 2007 a BBC headline announced that Arctic summers could be ice-free by 2013, quoting Wieslaw Maslowski. Lower in the same story, Mark Serreze, of America's snow and ice data centre, said Maslowski was probably a little aggressive, and that his own estimate was 2030. Summer ice is still there. But the trend is real: on 16 September 2012 satellites recorded a September minimum of 3.41 million square kilometres, about half the average September low of 1979 to 2000. A blown deadline is not a refuted trend.

A 1988 news report warned that rising seas could cover the Maldives within thirty years, and the islands are still there. A survey of every one of Tuvalu's 101 islands between 1971 and 2014, by Paul Kench and two colleagues, found that while local sea level rose about twice as fast as the global average, the nation's land area grew by about 3 percent, because reefs supplied sand and rubble faster than the sea climbed. Land area is not the same as a liveable home, though, and the Maldives is still building sea walls.

The 1970s cooling scare is another dated claim worth grading. In 1975 Newsweek's science writer Peter Gwynne warned of a cooling world; in 2014 he wrote that he had been over-enthusiastic, and that his old story did not make today's climate scientists wrong. The research papers were calmer than the magazines. When three researchers led by Thomas Peterson tallied every peer-reviewed temperature forecast published between 1965 and 1979, 71 in all, 44 pointed to warming, 7 to cooling, and 20 took no side.

Grading happens inside climate science too. In 2022 five scientists who accept human-caused warming, led by Zeke Hausfather, warned in Nature that about a fifth of the newest climate models run too hot, and that averaging all the models together drags the answer upward.

proving-that-species-can-vanish-cuvier-a.context_blurb:
Two hundred and fifty years ago most naturalists assumed that no kind of animal could ever vanish from creation. The French anatomist Georges Cuvier proved them wrong with bones, and a working-class fossil collector in England, Mary Anning, supplied some of the strangest proof.

In 1796 Cuvier compared the jaws and teeth of living Indian and African elephants with fossil mammoths from Siberia and the American "Ohio animal", later named the mastodon. They were four different species, and beasts that big could not be hiding unnoticed: whole kinds of animal had died out completely. Cuvier believed an animal's parts fit together as one working whole, so a single piece could reveal the rest, a rule he called the correlation of parts. From the skull of a huge skeleton dug up in Argentina he named a giant ground-dwelling sloth, Megatherium, the "great beast". In 1800, working only from a drawing of a fossil from Bavaria, he identified it as a little reptile that flew, the creature later called Pterodactylus.

At Lyme Regis, Mary Anning sold fossils to support her family and found some of the finest. When she unearthed a plesiosaur in 1823, its neck seemed so absurdly long that Cuvier suspected a forgery glued together from different animals. After Buckland and Conybeare supplied detailed drawings and evidence, he examined it and publicly withdrew the charge. Anning also worked out that the stony lumps found in the bellies of her ichthyosaurs, packed with fish scales and bones, were fossilised dung, and William Buckland named them coprolites in 1829. From them she could read who had eaten whom.

proving-the-gene-is-dna-griffith-avery-h.context_blurb:
In the early twentieth century most biologists thought genes must be made of protein. One reason was Phoebus Levene's 1909 picture of DNA: its four building blocks, the bases written A, C, G and T, repeating in one fixed unit, one of each, down the chain, far too monotonous to spell out a living thing. Three experiments between 1928 and 1952 pointed to DNA instead, and each was argued over, which is how the answer earned its place.

Frederick Griffith worked for Britain's health ministry as a medical officer, not as a geneticist. His job was to sort pneumococci, the bacteria behind many pneumonias, by type, because an antiserum made against one type did nothing against another. The deadly form wears a sugar coat, a capsule, that stops the body's white blood cells from swallowing it; the harmless form has lost its coat and is eaten at once. In 1928 Griffith gave mice a mixture of live harmless bacteria and heat-killed deadly ones. The mice died, and from their blood he cultured live, capsuled bacteria of exactly the deadly type he had heat-killed. Grown on in fresh broth, the line kept its capsule and its killing power through generation after generation, so something from the dead cells had become part of the living ones' inheritance. Griffith never learned what it was: in 1941 he was killed in his London flat by a German bomb in an air raid.

At the Rockefeller Institute, Maclyn McCarty, Colin MacLeod and their leader Oswald Avery spent years purifying Griffith's "transforming principle". Seventy-five litres of broth gave only 10 to 25 milligrams, a few fibrous threads. To identify it, they knocked out each suspect molecule in turn and watched which destruction killed the effect: protein-eating enzymes and an RNA-destroying enzyme left it working, but an enzyme that destroys DNA abolished it. In a 1943 letter to his brother, Avery wrote that it sounded like a virus and may be a gene. Their 1944 paper named a DNA fraction as the agent. Alfred Mirsky, a respected colleague at the same institute, objected for years that a few leftover protein molecules in the sample might be doing the work, a fair challenge, since a purification is only as good as what it leaves behind.

Alfred Hershey and his 24-year-old research assistant Martha Chase, just a year out of college, tested the question in 1952 with phages, viruses that infect bacteria. The trick used a chemical difference: DNA contains phosphorus but no sulfur, while protein contains sulfur but no phosphorus, so they labelled one batch of phage with radioactive phosphorus and another with radioactive sulfur. After the phages had attached and injected, they stripped the empty shells off the bacteria in a Waring blender, the kind sold for kitchens, run in bursts of a minute. Mostly phosphorus had gone in. When the infected bacteria burst, the new viruses carried 30 percent or more of their parents' phosphorus but less than 1 percent of their sulfur. Hershey and Chase still worded it cautiously: the protein probably had no function inside the cell, and the DNA had some function.

prusiners-infection-with-no-genes.context_blurb:
Stanley Prusiner, an American neurologist, argued from 1982 that a group of fatal brain diseases is spread by an infectious agent with no genes at all, a wrongly folded protein that he named the prion. Biologists called it heresy. Fifteen years later he won the Nobel Prize, and his idea still raises open questions about Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.

The heresy was against Francis Crick's central dogma of molecular biology, which says genetic information flows one way, from DNA to RNA to protein; a protein was supposed to be an end product, never a self-copying cause. Yet there were clues. In 1976 the American doctor Gajdusek won a Nobel Prize for showing that kuru, a fatal shaking illness in the highlands of Papua New Guinea, spread among the Fore through funeral customs in which relatives ate the brains of the dead.

Prusiner's mechanism is a matter of shape. The prion protein sits in every healthy brain in a coiled, harmless form. The dangerous form is the same molecule folded into flat sheets, and when it touches a healthy molecule it templates it into the same misfold, so what gets copied is a shape, not a code. The misfolded protein resists the enzymes that normally break proteins down, and it piles up in the brain.

Sceptics had a serious alternative: a virino, a tiny piece of nucleic acid wrapped in the host's own protein, too small or too shielded to detect. That was the right challenge to make, and it turned out to be wrong. When Prusiner's 1997 Nobel was announced, the laureate David Baltimore, a long-time doubter, called it one of the mythological stories of science: a scientist who kept faith through years of scorn and was finally shown to be right.

Genes still matter. Inherited mutations in a person's own prion-protein gene cause fatal familial insomnia and some forms of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease with no outside prion at all. And in mice, misfolded tau from Alzheimer's brains and alpha-synuclein from Parkinson's brains spread in a prion-like way, though whether that happens in patients is still an open question.

push-at-the-right-moment-resonance.context_blurb:
Everything that can wobble has a favourite rhythm, its natural frequency. Push it in step with that rhythm and small pushes pile up into huge swings; push out of step and they cancel. This is resonance, and it explains swings, singing glasses and falling bridges, though the true stories are messier than the textbook versions.

A father shoving a swing hard at random gets nowhere, while a small girl giving light taps can send her sister up to the top bar, because she times each tap to match the swing's own natural rhythm. The deciding variable is timing, not force. A singer who wants to shatter a wine glass must first find its note, the one it rings when you flick the rim with a fingernail, since only that pitch builds up the glass's flexing. It is hard in practice. On MythBusters in 2005 the vocal coach Jaime Vendera broke a glass with his unamplified voice at about 105 decibels, but only after trying a dozen glasses, and the engineer Jeffrey Kysar said it is possible only if you are both good and lucky.

Bridges feel it too. When a column of 74 soldiers crossed Broughton's suspension bridge outside Manchester on 12 April 1831, the deck began to bounce in time with their boots. Some of them found it funny, whistled a marching tune and stepped along with it. One corner of the deck collapsed into the river; nobody died, as the water was shallow. The investigators found the weak point was a single badly made bolt where a stay-chain was fixed to its anchor in the ground. Ever since, the British Army has told soldiers to fall out of step whenever they cross a bridge.

The 1850 collapse at Angers in France, which killed 226 of 483 soldiers, is often blamed on marching alone. The official inquiry blamed the men's rhythm together with a storm and corroded anchors on the bridge's main cables; the soldiers had even been told to break step. London's Millennium Bridge showed a stranger mechanism. When it opened in June 2000 the crowd was strolling, not marching, yet the deck swayed sideways because each walker unconsciously adjusted his stride to its motion, pushing it further, a loop in which the crowd drove its own bridge. Engineers cured it with dampers.

Engineers also turn timing against itself. A 660-tonne steel ball hangs inside the upper floors of Taipei 101. When the tower leans, the ball swings the opposite way, arriving just as the tower moves off, so each swing pulls against the building and soaks up the energy; in a 2015 typhoon it cut the sway by up to 40 percent. Not everything called resonance is resonance. Microwave ovens do not work by hitting a special frequency of water: the field grabs every lopsided molecule and twists it to and fro, and this works across a broad range of frequencies.

quantum-tunnelling-why-the-sun-shines-an.context_blurb:
In the everyday world a ball that lacks the energy to roll over a hill never reaches the other side. In the quantum world it sometimes does. A particle behaves like a wave, and a wave does not stop dead at a barrier but fades inside it, so if the barrier is thin some of the wave leaks through. This quantum tunnelling lights the Sun and stores your files.

At some fifteen million degrees, the Sun's core still leaves its protons far too feeble, by a factor of hundreds, to overcome their electric repulsion. They fuse anyway, because they go through the wall rather than over it. In 1920 Arthur Eddington proposed that stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium. Critics said stars were not hot enough, and their sums were right; Eddington replied that the critic should go and find a hotter place. He was right for a reason not discovered until years later. Even tunnelling is not the slow step: once two protons are jammed together, one of them must turn into a neutron during that instant, a rare weak-force event, so an average proton must wait billions of years for its turn, which is why the Sun lasts so long.

Tunnelling first explained radioactivity. In 1928 the young physicist George Gamow, visiting Göttingen, showed that an alpha particle trapped behind a nucleus's electric wall escapes by leaking through it as a wave, the effect now called quantum tunnelling; Ronald Gurney and Edward Condon found the same that year. The chance of getting through falls steeply as the barrier grows higher and wider and as the particle grows heavier, but it never quite reaches zero. That steepness solved a puzzle from 1911: polonium-212's alpha particles, with about twice the energy of uranium-238's, escape in a third of a microsecond, while uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years. The same steepness is why the effect is never seen with anything you can hold.

Tunnelling ticks inside molecules. In ammonia, the nitrogen atom tunnels back and forth through the flat triangle of its three hydrogen atoms, some 24 billion round trips each second, and in 1948 Harold Lyons used that rhythm to run the first atomic clock. In 1957 Leo Esaki and Yuriko Kurose, at the Tokyo firm soon renamed Sony, built a germanium junction in which turning up the voltage made the current fall, because electrons were tunnelling straight through; the tunnel diode was the first product built on the effect.

Tunnelling also lets us see atoms. In 1981 Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer at IBM in Zurich built the scanning tunnelling microscope. Its needle hovers a few atoms above a surface without touching it, and the instrument measures the electrons tunnelling across the empty gap. Widen the gap by just 0.1 nanometre and the current divides by ten, so a crude needle can sense heights far smaller than an atom. In 1989 Erhard Schweizer and Don Eigler used such a needle to place 35 xenon atoms one by one on chilled nickel, spelling out IBM in letters just five nanometres high.

Your flash drive depends on it. Each memory cell stores a bit as electrons parked on a floating gate, a scrap of conductor sealed inside an insulator with no wire attached; a strong electric field drives electrons through the insulator onto it, where they stay trapped for years. Tunnelling is also a headache. By its 65-nanometre chips Intel's gate insulators were only about five atoms thick and electrons leaked straight through, so in 2007 Intel swapped the material for a hafnium compound, cutting the leakage enormously.

rabies-and-the-boy-pasteur-was-not-allow.context_blurb:
Rabies was a death sentence once its symptoms began. In July 1885 Louis Pasteur tried an experimental treatment on a bitten boy, and its success made him a hero and paid for an institute. The full record, read a century later, shows that he gambled harder than he admitted.

On 6 July 1885 nine-year-old Joseph Meister arrived at Pasteur's Paris laboratory from Alsace. Two days earlier, on his way to school, he had been savaged by a rabid dog and bitten fourteen times. Pasteur, a chemist, held no medical licence, so it would have been illegal for him to inject a patient; the physician Jacques-Joseph Grancher gave the shots while Pasteur watched. There were thirteen over ten days, each made from the spinal cord of a rabbit that had died of rabies, dried and ground into a liquid. Cord dried for fewer days was stronger, so each dose was a little more potent than the last.

Treatment after a bite can work because the rabies agent travels slowly up the nerves to the brain, taking weeks, which gives the immune system time to learn. Modern post-bite treatment works the same way. Pasteur achieved all this without ever seeing his enemy. The culprit is a virus, much tinier than any bacterium and invisible to the microscopes of the day; he kept it alive only by passing it from rabbit to rabbit.

The case that made the treatment world-famous came months later. Jean-Baptiste Jupille, a fifteen-year-old shepherd, was bitten while fighting off a rabid dog with his whip and bare hands to protect younger children. He lived too. Donations poured in from around the world, and in 1888 the Institut Pasteur opened in Paris, a new research institute devoted to infectious disease.

When the historian Gerald Geison studied Pasteur's private notebooks, he reported in 1995 that before Meister, Pasteur had already tried the treatment on two patients, and one of them, a girl, had died. Meister himself later worked at the Institut as its caretaker. A legend says he shot himself in 1940 rather than open Pasteur's crypt to German soldiers, but a diary from the time and his granddaughter record that he took his own life with gas, convinced that his family had been seized; they returned hours after he died.

ramsay-finds-a-whole-column-nobody-suspe.context_blurb:
In the 1890s two British scientists found that the air we breathe holds a gas nobody had suspected, and then that it belonged to a whole family missing from the periodic table. The discovery began with a tiny difference in weight that one of them refused to ignore.

In 1892 Lord Rayleigh weighed a litre of nitrogen made by chemical reaction and a litre stripped from ordinary air. The air sample was heavier by about half a percent, and Rayleigh trusted his scales: the difference meant the air was hiding an unknown gas. Unable to explain it, he wrote a short letter to Nature, admitting he was much puzzled and inviting any reader to explain it.

The chemist William Ramsay took up the hunt, passing air-nitrogen over red-hot magnesium again and again until a small residue remained that reacted with nothing. In 1894 the two men announced a new gas, about one percent of the air, and named it argon, from the Greek for "lazy", because it refused to combine with anything. Henry Cavendish had seen the same stubborn bubble in 1785; he wrote it down faithfully and offered no explanation.

Argon had no home in the periodic table. Dmitri Mendeleev at first insisted it was a triple form of nitrogen, because a whole new column was something his table had never needed; he added one in 1902. More orphans followed. In 1895 Ramsay boiled the mineral cleveite in acid, and William Crookes found that the spectrum of the gas matched helium, known until then only from the Sun. In 1898 Ramsay and Morris Travers boiled off liquefied argon in stages and caught three more gases. One lit their tube with what Travers called a blaze of crimson light that he would never forget: neon.

Why are these noble gases so aloof? Their outermost shell of electrons is already full, so they have nothing to gain, lose or share. In 1904 the discovery earned two Nobel Prizes: Rayleigh took the physics prize and Ramsay the chemistry prize.

reading-a-climate-nobody-wrote-down.context_blurb:
Nobody kept weather records during the ice ages, yet scientists can read past climates from boulders, tree rings and bubbles of ancient air locked in ice. Each record has its own strengths and its own traps, and reading them honestly means admitting both.

In the 1830s Louis Agassiz argued from stray boulders and scratched bedrock that glaciers had once covered Europe. William Buckland, Britain's leading champion of the idea that such marks came from Noah's Flood, toured Scotland with Agassiz in 1840 and changed his mind. When Agassiz presented his case for glaciers to the Geological Society, Buckland, presiding, rose after him with a paper of his own in support. Agassiz could show that ice had been there but not why it came. In 1864 the Scot James Croll proposed shifts in Earth's orbit, and he named the weakness himself: the orbital nudge alone was much too weak to grow ice sheets, and it would need the climate itself to amplify it.

Tree rings are another archive. The astronomer A. E. Douglass started measuring ring widths in Arizona pines in 1901, hoping to find the Sun's sunspot rhythm recorded in the wood; instead he founded tree-ring dating. Rings have traps too. Tree-ring density at hundreds of northern sites had tracked measured summer temperatures closely, but Keith Briffa's team reported in 1998 that from around 1960 onward the wood's density dropped even as thermometers recorded warming. A proxy that fails where we can check it is a warning for the centuries where we cannot.

Ice is the most direct record, because its bubbles are actual samples of old air. In 1965 the French glaciologist Claude Lorius, chilling his whisky with ice cut from the Antarctic sheet, watched it fizz and realised, by his own account, that the bubbles were air from the distant past, trapped at the moment that snow had settled. Year layers can be counted in the upper ice, since summer layers hold bigger bubbles than winter ones. But snow stays porous for 50 to 120 metres, so trapped air is always younger than its icy prison: at a dry site like Vostok the ice may be about 6,000 years old before its bubbles close. Russian drillers at Vostok reached 3,623 metres in 1996, covering more than 400,000 years, and then stopped with good ice still below, because a sealed lake lay underneath and their drilling fluid would have polluted it. The oldest ice yet dated, 2.7 million years, came from near the surface at the Allan Hills, where moving ice is pushed upward against hidden hills and the wind scours away the new snow.

Ice also records the timing of carbon dioxide and warming. In 2003 Nicolas Caillon's team, reading temperature and CO2 from the same trapped air at Vostok, found that at the thaw about 240,000 years ago the CO2 increase trailed the start of Antarctic warming by some 800 years. They read that as CO2 amplifying a warming begun by Earth's orbit, and they contrasted it with today's rise, which, they wrote, had clearly been imposed first, by human activity. In 2013 Parrenin's team used a better clock on the most recent thaw and found the two moving together: CO2 ahead by just 10 years, with an uncertainty of 160. Different thaws give different answers, and the numbers are still argued over.

red-cabbage-litmus-and-the-ladder-of-ten.context_blurb:
Acids and bases are everywhere, from lemon juice to drain cleaner, and you can measure them with a vegetable. The story of how chemists learned to tell them apart runs from medieval medicine to a Danish brewery, and much of it can be tested in a kitchen.

Boil chopped red cabbage and strain off the purple water. Its pigments change shape as they gain or lose hydrogen ions: acid turns the juice red-pink and neutral water leaves it purple, while rising alkalinity carries it through blue and green to yellow. Baking soda is only mildly alkaline, so it turns the juice blue and no further; reaching green and yellow takes something caustic like drain cleaner, which only an adult should handle.

Plant indicators are old. Around 1300 the Catalan physician Arnaldus de Villa Nova used litmus, a dye from lichens, to tell acids from bases while preparing medicines. In 1664 Robert Boyle made such tests systematic. Others had watched sour liquors redden the blue syrup and credited something special in those liquors; Boyle tried everything in his laboratory and reported that almost any acid salt reddens the syrup, so the colour change marked a whole class of substances. The alkalis that turned the syrup green included distillations of blood, urine and the horn of deer, as well as mineral ones. He told readers to check it themselves by putting a drop of the syrup onto white paper, so the change would show clearly and use little syrup: an early test strip.

Sørensen, chief chemist at the Carlsberg brewery's laboratory in Copenhagen, created the pH scale in 1909 to express acidity as a single short number. The scale is logarithmic: each step means ten times as many free hydrogen ions. So hungry stomach juice, at about pH 1.7, holds roughly half a million times as many free hydrogen ions as blood, which stays near pH 7.4.

Svante Arrhenius explained why acids behave as they do, arguing that acids and salts split into charged particles in water. His examiners at Uppsala in 1884 gave the thesis the lowest passing mark, non sine laude approbatur; he won the 1903 Nobel Prize for it. The old rule said a base must contain hydroxide, but ammonia has none and still makes water strongly alkaline. The hydroxide comes from the water: the water hands a hydrogen ion to the ammonia, and hydroxide is left behind. In 1923 Johannes Brønsted and Thomas Lowry, independently, redefined acids as givers of hydrogen ions and bases as takers.

Some tests need only a scale. Mix vinegar and baking soda in an open cup on a kitchen scale and the reading falls; seal the same mixture in a freezer bag and it does not move, because the carbon dioxide escapes from the open cup but has nowhere to go in the bag. Litmus paper is blunter than cabbage juice, purple across a wide middle range, because it blends ten to fifteen different lichen dyes, and each one changes colour at a different point. No indicator can be sharper than about two pH units, because the eye reads one colour cleanly only once one form of the dye makes up about nine parts in ten of the mixture. Even carbonic acid, the fizz in soda water, holds a surprise: in water it falls apart within microseconds, but calculations say a dry molecule, with no water to help break it, would last about 180,000 years.

resistance-evolution-you-can-watch-in-a-.context_blurb:
Antibiotics changed medicine, and bacteria have been fighting back ever since. Antibiotic resistance is evolution by natural selection fast enough to watch: the drug kills the vulnerable, and the rare survivors inherit the field.

Alexander Fleming saw it coming. In his 1945 Nobel lecture he imagined a Mr X who takes too little penicillin for a sore throat and breeds resistant germs, which then kill his wife; the one to blame for her death, Fleming said, was Mr X himself. His moral: if you use penicillin, use enough. Most people still misunderstand how resistance works. In a 2015 World Health Organization survey across twelve countries, 76 percent thought that a patient's own body grows resistant to the medicine; in fact it is the bacteria that change, and they spread to other people.

In 2016 Michael Baym and Roy Kishony made it visible on a giant dish as big as a table, poured in bands of antibiotic, each ten times stronger than the last toward the middle. E. coli released at the edges stalled at each new band until one cell happened on a mutation that let it grow there, and its descendants spread into the stronger band as a fan from a single point. Beginning with zero resistance, the bacteria crossed to a centre band holding 3,000 times the normal killing dose of trimethoprim in about ten days. Family trees of the lineages held a surprise: the most resistant mutants were often stuck behind the lineages leading the advance, hemmed in with nowhere to grow.

Bacteria resist in a few concrete ways. Some make beta-lactamases, a family of more than 2,000 enzymes that cut open the central ring shared by penicillin and its relatives, leaving the drug dead. Some use pumps: E. coli's AcrAB-TolC spans the cell wall and bails antibiotics of three different families back out as fast as they come in. Others change the target. MRSA, the staph that shrugged off methicillin within a year of its 1960 debut, carries a borrowed gene, mecA, for a replacement wall-building protein that the drug cannot latch onto.

Resistance genes also jump between species. Many bacteria hold extra rings of DNA, called plasmids, beside their chromosome, and one cell can pass a copy to a neighbour through a thin tube it extends, spreading resistance far faster than new mutations arise. In 2002 a Michigan dialysis patient's staph became resistant to vancomycin, the drug of last resort, after picking up the vanA gene from an Enterococcus infecting her at the same time.

Resistance is ancient, because antibiotics are ancient weapons of soil microbes. A bacterium from Lechuguilla Cave in New Mexico, sealed from the surface for over four million years, resisted 26 of 40 modern antibiotics, across fourteen drug classes. Vanessa D'Costa's team rebuilt a resistance gene from 30,000-year-old permafrost, and its protein worked against vancomycin just like the gene found in hospitals today. Even familiar advice is being tested. In 2017 Martin Llewelyn and colleagues argued in the BMJ that the ideal length of treatment has never been worked out for most infections, so courses should be set by doctors for each patient; their point was not that you should cut your own course short.

ritters-ultraviolet-the-other-invisible-.context_blurb:
In 1800 William Herschel found invisible rays beyond the red edge of a rainbow of sunlight by laying a thermometer there. A year later a young German, Johann Wilhelm Ritter, went looking past the violet end and found ultraviolet light with a strip of chemically treated paper.

Ritter's hunch came from philosophy. He was part of Naturphilosophie, a German Romantic school of thought which held that nature is built of opposites, so he reasoned that Herschel's heat rays past red must be balanced by an opposite kind of ray past violet. A hunch is not evidence, but this one pointed somewhere real. He could not copy Herschel, because the light beyond violet brings almost no warmth, and a thermometer would hardly react. Instead, on 22 February 1801, he laid paper soaked in silver chloride, which darkens in light, beyond the violet edge of a prism's spectrum. It darkened faster there than in any visible colour: he had found ultraviolet light, which he called chemical rays.

Ultraviolet does damage that much warmer light cannot. A red heat lamp can warm your face for hours, while twenty minutes of noon sun can burn it, because each particle of ultraviolet light carries more energy, enough to snap the chemical bonds in skin. Window glass does not fully protect you. A 2012 photograph in the New England Journal of Medicine showed a delivery driver whose left side of the face, beside the closed truck window for 28 years, looked decades older than the right: glass blocks the shorter UVB rays but lets the longer UVA rays straight through, and UVA ages the skin.

Ritter paid for his own experiments. For years he ran the poles of electric batteries across his own eyes, tongue and nose, and took opium to dull the effects. He died in Munich in 1810, aged 33 and deep in debt.

roentgens-hand-of-bones.context_blurb:
On 8 November 1895, in his laboratory at Würzburg in Germany, the physicist Wilhelm Roentgen noticed a glow that should not have been there. Within weeks he had found rays that pass through flesh and show the bones beneath, and within months doctors around the world were using them. Their dangers took longer to learn.

Roentgen had wrapped his discharge tube in black cardboard so that no light could escape and darkened the room, yet a little screen coated with barium platinocyanide, two metres away, glowed a faint green whenever the tube was on. The cardboard ruled out ordinary light. Cathode rays, which he had studied for years, bend in a magnet, but when he brought a strong magnet up to these rays they did not bend at all. Not knowing what they were, he called them X-rays, for the unknown. For seven weeks he told almost no one; he lived in his laboratory, eating and sleeping there while he tested what the rays would pass through. A thousand-page book barely stopped them, but 1.5 millimetres of lead did. When an American journalist later asked what he had thought on first seeing the glow, Roentgen answered that he did not stop to think, he investigated.

Weeks earlier he had already seen living bones, as a moving shadow on the glowing fluorescent screen, before his wife Anna Bertha pressed her hand to a photographic plate on 22 December for about fifteen minutes; it showed the bones of her fingers and her wedding ring.

He published on 28 December and refused to take out any patent, wanting everyone to benefit, so within six weeks machines were running in Montreal and New Hampshire. In Montreal in February 1896, John Cox spent forty-five minutes making a plate of Tolson Cunning's leg that showed a bullet surgeons had failed to find. It was removed, and the plate was then carried into a courtroom as evidence at the trial of the man who had shot him. At Roentgen's only public lecture on the rays, in January 1896, the anatomist Albert von Kölliker, whose hand had just been X-rayed in front of the audience, proposed that the rays be named after Roentgen, to general cheering. In 1901 Roentgen won the first Nobel Prize in Physics and gave the money to his university, but he was so shy of speaking that he declined to give the Nobel lecture.

An X-ray tube makes its rays by braking: electrons hurled across tens of thousands of volts slam into a metal target and give off X-rays as they are pulled up short. Less than one percent of the energy becomes X-rays and the rest is heat, so high-power tubes turn the tungsten target into a rapidly spinning disc, thousands of turns a minute, spreading the heat around a ring. Bone shows up because the power of an atom to absorb X-rays climbs with the cube of its atomic number, so calcium, number 20, stops far more of the beam than the light elements of flesh, and lead, number 82, stops it almost entirely.

The danger was learned slowly. Thomas Edison's glassblower Clarence Dally tested X-ray tubes on his own hands for years, lost both arms and died in 1904; Edison gave up the work and said outright that he was afraid of the rays. Even so, by about 1950 some ten thousand American shoe shops had X-ray cabinets in which a child could watch the bones of his feet inside a new shoe, with three viewing ports on top for the child, the parent and the clerk. States began banning them in 1957.

rule-by-the-experts-technocracy-inc-to-o.context_blurb:
Can experts with enough data run a society better than the people living in it? In the twentieth century that question was put to the test: in a Depression-era movement of engineers, in a famous parable about a shared pasture, and in twenty years of fieldwork by an American political scientist who went and looked.

During the Depression winter of 1932-33, with a quarter of Americans out of work, a movement called Technocracy promised to abolish politicians, businessmen and money and hand the continent to engineers. Its leader, Howard Scott, would have replaced the dollar with energy certificates, a ration measured in units of energy, which expired if unspent. It was his second try. His first group, the Technical Alliance, set up in 1919 to tally all the energy North America made and wasted, dissolved in 1921 without finishing the survey. The data a planner needs can be bigger than the planner. Technocracy itself faded after the press ridiculed Scott's 1933 radio address.

The economist Friedrich Hayek had named the deeper problem in a 1945 essay on how knowledge is used in society: the knowledge a central planner would need is scattered among millions of people, local and often never written down.

In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin published "The Tragedy of the Commons", a parable of herdsmen sharing a pasture open to all. Each adds one more animal, because he keeps the whole gain while everyone shares the cost, until the pasture is ruined. Critics noticed what the parable quietly assumes: that the herdsmen cannot talk to one another, watch one another or punish cheats, which no real village is like.

Elinor Ostrom did not argue on paper. She and her students spent some twenty years tramping through actual meadows, woodlands and irrigation canals, from Swiss alpine pastures to the canals of Valencia, and reading the rulebooks villages had written for them. Many communities had managed shared resources for centuries without either private ownership or a state. In 2009 she shared the economics Nobel, the first woman ever to win it. Open resources without rules really can collapse as Hardin described; the lesson is that it depends on the rules people make.

rumford-bores-a-cannon-and-the-caloric-f.context_blurb:
In the 1790s most scientists thought heat was caloric, an invisible, weightless fluid that flowed from hot things to cold and could never be made or destroyed. Count Rumford, an American-born adventurer running the arsenal in Munich, tested that idea with a cannon, two horses and a box of water.

Rumford was born Benjamin Thompson in Woburn, Massachusetts, fled Boston as a suspected Loyalist in 1776, and turned up in Bavaria as a count who fed the Munich poor on a cheap soup. Heat was his lifelong passion: he designed an efficient fireplace and invented thermal underwear. Caloric was then respectable chemistry. In 1789 Antoine Lavoisier listed 33 simple substances that could not be broken down, and beside oxygen and hydrogen the list included caloric and light.

While overseeing the boring of cannon at the Munich arsenal, Rumford noticed how hot the brass grew, and found by experiment that the metal chips cut off by the borer were hotter than boiling water. So he built a test. He sealed a brass gun barrel in a wooden box of cold water and had horses turn it against a deliberately blunt steel borer, because a dull tool rubs and grinds where a sharp one cuts, turning far more of the horses' work into heat. Two and a half hours later, with no fire anywhere, the water was boiling hard, to the astonishment of the onlookers.

Rumford then shut every escape route for caloric. Could the heat have flowed in from the surrounding water? No: the water was itself growing hotter, and a body cannot give heat to the very thing it is taking heat from. Could boring have squeezed caloric out of the brass by turning it into chips? He heated chips and solid slips of the same brass equally, dropped each into equal amounts of cold water, and both warmed their water by exactly the same amount, so the chips held just as much heat as the solid metal. The heat seemed inexhaustible, lasting as long as the horses walked. Rumford's conclusion was a principle: anything an insulated body can keep supplying without limit cannot possibly be a material substance, and heat, he argued, must be motion.

He also attacked his own result: one horse could have turned the machine, and burning the hay needed to feed that horse would have produced more heat than all the boring. Half a century later James Joule used Rumford's figures to estimate how much work makes a given amount of heat, and got a number too high by about a third, because Rumford had not counted the heat soaked into the wooden box and lost to the room.

Caloric did not die at once. A popular story says Humphry Davy clinched the case in 1799 by rubbing ice together inside a vacuum until it melted, but Nature corrected it twice: Davy rubbed the ice in open air, and his vacuum trial was a separate one using wax. In 1824 Sadi Carnot still reasoned with caloric, picturing it falling from hot to cold like water turning a mill wheel, with the temperature difference playing the part of the waterfall's height, and from that wrong picture he derived a true limit on engine efficiency. A model that predicts correctly is not thereby true.

rust-fire-running-in-slow-motion.context_blurb:
Rust is burning in slow motion. The same chemistry that makes steel wool flare in a flame eats a garden gate over a winter, and simple kitchen experiments can show what it needs and how to stop it.

Put one iron nail in dry air with a drying agent, one under a layer of oil in water that has been boiled, and one half-covered in tap water. After two weeks only the last one has rusted, because rust needs oxygen and water together, and neither alone will do. Rusting and burning steel wool are the same reaction, iron combining with oxygen. Steel wool's huge surface lets the reaction run away and glow, while a solid gate rusts too slowly ever to get hot enough to glow. Weigh a wad of steel wool, burn it, weigh it again, and the black residue weighs more, not less, because the iron has pulled oxygen out of the air and locked it in; weighings like this helped Lavoisier overturn the phlogiston theory.

Not every oxide is harmful. Aluminium reacts with oxygen as readily as iron, but its oxide forms a thin, tight film that seals the metal, while iron's rust is flaky and porous, so it falls away and exposes fresh iron to attack. The Statue of Liberty's copper skin is only 2.4 millimetres thick, yet after more than a century in salty harbour air it has lost very little, because its green patina of copper carbonates and sulfates is a stable layer that shields the copper beneath.

Rusting is also electrical. On wet iron one patch gives up iron and electrons while a nearby patch uses those electrons to combine oxygen with water, and the film of water carries ions between them, like a tiny battery; salt makes that water conduct better and speeds the rust. Ships use the battery against itself. Blocks of zinc bolted to steel hulls corrode away instead of the steel, because zinc gives up electrons more readily than iron, so the surface battery eats the zinc and spares the hull.

rutherfords-gold-foil-the-shell-that-bou.context_blurb:
In 1909, in Ernest Rutherford's laboratory at Manchester, a young student fired alpha particles at a thin sheet of gold and saw a few of them bounce straight back. From that surprise Rutherford worked out that every atom has a tiny, heavy centre, the nucleus, and is otherwise almost empty.

Rutherford, born in New Zealand, had already won the 1908 Nobel Prize, oddly in chemistry, and he joked at the dinner that the quickest transformation he had ever seen had been his own transformation from physicist to chemist. At Manchester, Hans Geiger asked for a small research task for his student Ernest Marsden, and Rutherford suggested looking for alpha particles scattered through large angles, though he expected none at all to return. The detector was a human eye: Marsden sat in a blacked-out room watching a zinc-sulfide screen through a microscope and counting each faint flash as an alpha struck it. Gold was the favourite target because no other metal can be hammered as thin, so a big swerve could be blamed on a single atom.

J. J. Thomson's atom, the standard picture then, spread its positive charge evenly through the whole atom, and a charge spread that thin could only nudge a fast alpha: it predicted a blur of a couple of degrees and nothing more. Yet a few alphas turned right round. The figure everyone quotes, one in 8,000 bouncing back, actually came from a thicker foil of platinum; gold's rate was nearer one in 20,000. In a 1936 lecture Rutherford compared the moment to firing a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and having it come back and hit you, a line he spoke 27 years later, not at the bench.

In 1911 Rutherford reasoned that the atom keeps nearly all its weight, and all its positive charge, in a minute central core. Enlarge an atom until it is as wide as a football pitch, a hundred metres across, and the nucleus is a grain of sand half a millimetre across, sitting on the centre spot. To test the idea, Geiger and Marsden rebuilt the experiment in 1913 and counted over 100,000 flashes by eye, at two or three a minute, and the numbers matched Rutherford's prediction at every angle. Thomson's model, often mocked as the plum pudding, never got that name from Thomson; the phrase first appeared in a pharmacists' trade paper, The Chemist and Druggist, in 1906.

In 1919 Rutherford fired alphas into nitrogen and knocked out protons, the first deliberate transmutation of one element into another. Patrick Blackett took about 400,000 cloud-chamber photographs of alpha particles in 1925, and the eight that caught the reaction showed the alpha staying inside the nucleus: nitrogen had become oxygen.

Rutherford's atom had a flaw: by classical physics an electron circling the nucleus should radiate away its energy and spiral inward almost at once. In 1913 Niels Bohr, who had worked in Manchester, added a rule that only certain orbits are allowed, and that an electron in one of them never radiates. Textbooks say Rutherford himself admitted the instability, but in 2022 Nils-Erik Bomark and Reidun Renstrom read his 1911 paper line by line and reported that he never discussed the electrons' motion at all; other accounts read it differently, and the paper is short enough to check yourself.

sagans-dragon-in-the-garage.context_blurb:
In The Demon-Haunted World, his 1995 book on thinking clearly, the astronomer Carl Sagan imagined a friend who insists that a dragon, breathing fire, lives in his garage. Every test you propose meets an excuse: a camera fails because she is invisible, flour on the floor fails because she floats, an infrared sensor fails because her fire gives no heat. So Sagan asked what difference there is between such a dragon and no dragon at all. Each excuse appears only after a test is proposed, and a claim rebuilt to dodge every test has stopped predicting anything, so no one can check it.

In the same book Sagan offered a set of tools for spotting bad arguments, which he called the baloney detection kit: seek independent confirmation, welcome debate, consider several explanations, do not get attached to your own, check every link in the chain, and ask whether a claim could in principle be proved false. At its heart, he wrote, are two habits held together: an openness to new ideas, however strange, joined to ruthless scrutiny of every one; drop either, and science breaks down.

Sagan made famous the line that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, on Cosmos in 1980. The sociologist Marcello Truzzi had written almost the same words two years earlier, and the idea goes back to Pierre-Simon Laplace around 1810.

same-note-different-instrument-harmonics.context_blurb:
A trumpet, a violin and a flute can play exactly the same note and still sound nothing alike. The difference, called timbre, comes from the fainter, higher notes, the harmonics, that ride on top of the main note, and from how each sound begins. Scientists spent three centuries working out how it works, and part of the answer lives in the brain.

Orchestras tune to an A of 440 vibrations a second, but nothing in physics picks that number: it was a 1936 recommendation of the American Standards Association, and baroque groups still tune lower. A plucked string vibrates in many shapes at once: as a whole, in halves, in thirds and so on. Rest a fingertip lightly at the exact middle of a guitar string, pluck it and lift the finger, and a clean note one octave higher than normal rings out, because only the shapes with a still point at the middle survive. A tuning fork sounds almost pure because its next possible note lies more than six times higher than its main one and takes up very little energy.

In 1636 the French friar Marin Mersenne measured real strings and printed their rules. Pitch rises with tension, but only with its square root, so it takes four times the pull to double a string's pitch. Much of an instrument's identity lies in how each note begins: record a trumpet and a piano, trim away the opening instant of each note while leaving the steady sound untouched, and listeners struggle far more to tell which instrument is which. A bare string moves little air. On a violin, the bridge passes its shaking to the wooden body, and the air shut inside the body also resonates, sloshing in and out through the f-holes like air in a blown bottle. In the 1860s Hermann von Helmholtz listed the harmonics hidden in real tones with no machine at all. He used hollow brass and glass spheres, each tuned to one pitch, and pressed the small neck of each into his own ear, so that it boomed when its note was present.

A clarinet behaves oddly. Its register key makes a low note leap not an octave but a twelfth, to three times the starting frequency. The reason is its shape: a clarinet's tube is a straight cylinder, closed at the reed end, while the oboe's and saxophone's tubes widen into cones. A closed cylinder sounds mainly the odd-numbered harmonics, which gives the clarinet its hollow voice and rules out the octave jump.

Joseph Fourier showed in 1807 that any repeating wave is a sum of pure sine waves, and he found it while studying the way heat moves through solid objects, not music. Then came a puzzle. In the 1840s August Seebeck used a siren, a whirling perforated disc that chops a jet of air, to make a sound with no vibration at its low repeating rate, only higher components, yet listeners plainly heard that missing low note. Helmholtz blamed a distortion made inside the ear. J. C. R. Licklider tested the idea in 1954 by burying the tones in noise loud enough to drown anything the ear might add, and the low pitch remained, so the brain was working it out from the harmonics. Phones use the trick: a tiny speaker cannot make deep bass, so processing adds a stack of the higher harmonics of the bass note and lets your brain supply the missing low pitch.

schrodingers-cat-was-a-rebuke.context_blurb:
Schrödinger's cat, alive and dead at once, is usually quoted as a celebration of quantum weirdness. Its author meant the opposite. Erwin Schrödinger, an Austrian physicist, built the thought experiment in 1935 to show how absurd one reading of quantum theory becomes when applied to everyday objects.

The imagined box held a cat, a Geiger counter, a speck of radioactive material with an even chance of one atom decaying within the hour, a relay, a hammer and a glass vial of hydrocyanic acid, a cyanide poison, which the hammer would smash if the atom decayed. Read literally, the Copenhagen interpretation's rules for measurement put the cat in a blend of alive and dead until someone looks; Schrödinger called the case ridiculous and aimed it squarely at that interpretation. Albert Einstein had egged him on: in a letter earlier that year he described a keg of gunpowder that quantum mechanics would treat as a mixture of exploded and unexploded.

In the same paper Schrödinger named what he considered the defining feature of quantum theory: entanglement, the linking of particles so that measuring one fixes the other. His German word, Verschränkung, came from joinery, where it names the dovetail, two boards locked together with wedge-shaped teeth. For decades the paper was barely read, drawing only about 26 citations in its first forty years; today entanglement is the raw material of quantum computers.

A real cat could never stay in such a blend. Every moment it trades light and air molecules with everything around it, and that contact drains the superposition out into its surroundings in well under a billionth of a second, a process called decoherence. Serge Haroche's group in Paris watched it happen on a tiny scale, trapping a few microwave photons bouncing between superconducting mirrors in a superposition and watching it fall apart step by step; Haroche shared the 2012 Nobel Prize for it. Why one particular outcome appears in the end, the measurement problem, is still debated.

screening-embryos-from-disease-to-specif.context_blurb:
Couples using IVF can now have their embryos tested before one is chosen for transfer. The technique began in 1989 at Hammersmith Hospital in London, to help families avoid passing on serious inherited disease, and it has since spread toward ranking embryos on predicted traits, where the science is far weaker.

Embryo tests come in three kinds. The first, PGT-M, hunts for one particular faulty gene that runs in the family, such as the cystic fibrosis gene; for families carrying a disease like Huntington's, choosing an embryo free of it is a genuine mercy. Another, PGT-A, counts chromosomes, checking whether the embryo has the right number, since a missing or extra one usually means miscarriage. The third gives each embryo a polygenic score from thousands of common DNA variants to predict a trait. Such scores are built from differences among unrelated people, but brothers and sisters share on average about half of their variable DNA, so embryos from one couple differ much less, and Shai Carmi's team showed in 2019 that picking the top-ranked embryo gains very little. That has not stopped the market. In 2024 an undercover Guardian investigation found the US start-up Heliospect Genomics offering to rank a couple's embryos by predicted IQ, for about $50,000. Selecting embryos on predicted IQ is illegal in Britain.

seeing-one-atom-and-then-picking-it-up.context_blurb:
For most of history atoms were an idea no one could see. In 1955 a physicist at Penn State finally saw them, and within forty years scientists could not only image single atoms but push them around and photograph the waves of electrons between them.

In 1955 Erwin Müller and his student Kanwar Bahadur chilled a needle-sharp tungsten tip, let in helium gas, and watched bright dots appear on a screen in neat rings: they were the first people to see individual atoms directly. Müller is said to have shouted at the screen in delight.

A different instrument rests on a quantum effect. In classical physics a particle lacking the energy to get over a barrier simply bounces back, but in quantum mechanics it has a small chance of slipping straight through, which is called tunnelling. In 1981 Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer at IBM in Zurich held a needle just above a surface so that electrons tunnelled across the gap. Their scanning tunnelling microscope kept that current constant as the needle swept across, so the needle's rise and fall traced the bumps of individual atoms. Strictly these are not photographs: each image is assembled from measurements of tunnelling current, with no light or lens involved.

The same needle could move atoms. In 1989 Don Eigler and Erhard Schweizer dragged 35 xenon atoms across cold nickel to spell the company's three letters, IBM. In 1993 Eigler's group set out a ring of 48 iron atoms on copper, a quantum corral, and the image showed circular ripples inside it: the waves of electrons trapped by the ring, a wavefunction made visible. Leo Gross's team at IBM Zurich went further in 2009, fixing one molecule of carbon monoxide to the tip of an atomic-force microscope and imaging every bond in a pentacene molecule.

semmelweis-and-the-two-wards.context_blurb:
In the 1840s, at the Vienna General Hospital, childbed fever was killing new mothers in terrible numbers, but far more in one maternity clinic than in the one next door. The doctor Ignaz Semmelweis counted, compared and found the cause, years before anyone knew germs existed, and his profession punished him for it.

The two clinics were next-door neighbours that admitted women on alternating days, so the calendar alone decided where a woman gave birth. In the First Clinic, run by physicians and medical students, mothers died at several times the rate of the Second Clinic, run by midwives. Women knew it. Some begged on their knees not to be admitted to the First Clinic, and some gave birth in the street and then arrived claiming it had happened on the way.

Semmelweis, an assistant in the First Clinic from 1846, tested the explanations on offer. Crowding could not be the cause, because the hospital's records showed the safer midwives' clinic was always the more crowded. He had his own wrong ideas too: for a time he blamed the priest who walked through the ward to give the last rites, frightening the women. Then he compared the two staffs' days, and one difference stood out: the doctors and students spent their mornings dissecting corpses in the pathology room and went straight from there to the delivery beds, while the midwives never touched the dead.

The clue came in March 1847, when his friend Jakob Kolletschka died after a student accidentally cut his finger with a scalpel during an autopsy. Kolletschka's body showed the same findings as the dead mothers. Semmelweis concluded that the doctors carried what he called cadaverous particles, decaying matter from the dead, on their hands; he knew nothing of bacteria. In May 1847 he ordered every hand scrubbed with chlorinated lime before examinations, because chlorine, unlike soap, got rid of the stench of the corpses, and that smell was his only way to tell whether a hand was clean. The First Clinic's death rate fell from 18.3 percent in April to about 2 percent in June.

He was not the first. In 1843 Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr had argued in Boston that physicians spread childbed fever from one mother to the next. The Philadelphia obstetrician Charles Meigs answered with no evidence at all: doctors are gentlemen, he wrote, and a gentleman's hands are clean. Vienna dismissed Semmelweis in 1849. In the maternity ward of St Rókus in Pest he imposed the same rule, and over four years his ward delivered 933 babies and lost only eight mothers to childbed fever, a replication in a new hospital with new staff.

When his 1861 book on childbed fever was shrugged off, he published open letters attacking named opponents as murderers, which turned colleagues against him. In 1865 he was taken to an asylum near Vienna, where guards beat him, and he died two weeks later from blood poisoning that spread from a gangrenous wound on his right hand, the same kind of infection that had killed his patients. His name now labels the Semmelweis reflex: the knee-jerk dismissal of fresh evidence simply because it clashes with what everyone already believes.
